chapters.n: Exodus opens by linking back to Genesis: these are the sons of Israel (Jacob) who came to Egypt with their families. The story of a family now becomes the story of a nation.

f.g: The Hebrew title of Exodus is Shemot, “Names,” from this opening line.

chapters.n: The sons of Leah are listed first, beginning with Reuben, the firstborn.
Leah’s other two sons, then Benjamin, Rachel’s son, are named. Joseph is left out because he was already in Egypt.
The sons of the handmaids Bilhah and Zilpah complete the list of tribal fathers.

f.w: Dan, and Naphtali, Gad, and Asher

chapters.n: Seventy people in all descended from Jacob—a small family that will grow into a great nation, as God promised.
Joseph, his brothers, and their whole generation died. The memory of Joseph’s great service would soon fade.
Israel multiplied enormously—the words echo God’s creation command to “be fruitful and multiply.” God’s promise to Abraham was being fulfilled even in a foreign land.

f.w: were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied

chapters.n: A new king rose who did not know—or chose not to honor—what Joseph had done for Egypt. The tide turns against Israel.
The new Pharaoh stirred up fear: the Israelites are too many and too strong. Fear of “the other” often leads to oppression.
He proposed “dealing shrewdly” with them, fearing they might side with an enemy in war and leave Egypt—ironically exactly what would happen.

f.w: get them up out of the land

chapters.n: Egypt forced the Israelites into hard labor under harsh supervisors, building storage cities for Pharaoh.
The more Egypt oppressed them, the more Israel grew. God’s blessing could not be stopped. The Egyptians came to dread them.
The Egyptians made Israel work ruthlessly.
Their lives were made bitter with brickmaking, mortar, and field labor. The bitter herbs of the Passover would later recall this bitterness.
Pharaoh turned to the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah. Scripture remembers their names while the mighty Pharaoh remains unnamed.
Pharaoh secretly ordered them to kill every Hebrew baby boy at birth but let the girls live.

f.g: birthing stones or stool used in childbirth

chapters.n: The midwives feared God more than Pharaoh and refused to obey. This is one of the earliest recorded acts of civil disobedience for conscience’ sake.
Pharaoh summoned the midwives and demanded to know why the boys were alive.
The midwives explained that Hebrew women were so vigorous they gave birth before help arrived—a clever answer that protected the babies.
God blessed the midwives, and Israel kept growing stronger.
Because they feared God, He gave them families of their own. Those who protect life are blessed with life.
Pharaoh then commanded all his people to throw every Hebrew baby boy into the Nile. It is into this terror that Moses will be born.
A man and woman of the tribe of Levi married. Later we learn their names: Amram and Jochebed. From this priestly tribe comes Israel’s deliverer.

f.w: a man of the house of Levi

chapters.n: Their son was born under Pharaoh’s death decree. Seeing he was a “goodly” child—the same word God used to call creation “good”—his mother hid him for three months.
When she could no longer hide him, she made a small waterproof basket of papyrus, sealed it, and set it among the reeds of the Nile. The word for “ark” is the same as Noah’s ark—a vessel of rescue.

f.g: Hebrew tevah — used only here and for Noah’s ark

chapters.n: His older sister—Miriam—watched from a distance to see what would happen.
Pharaoh’s own daughter came to bathe and spotted the basket. She sent her maid to bring it.
Seeing the crying baby, she felt compassion and realized he was a Hebrew child. Compassion crossed the lines her father had drawn.
Miriam boldly offered to find a Hebrew woman to nurse the baby for the princess.
The princess agreed, and Miriam brought the baby’s own mother.
Pharaoh’s daughter paid Moses’s mother to nurse her own son. God turned the danger into protection and provision.
When weaned, the child was adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter. She named him Moses, explaining, “I drew him out of the water.” Moses would later draw Israel through the water.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew mashah, “to draw out”; also similar to an Egyptian word meaning “son.”

chapters.n: As a grown man, Moses went out to see his own people, the Hebrews, and saw their suffering. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew.
Moses looked around, killed the Egyptian, and hid the body in the sand. He acted out of zeal for justice, but in his own way and timing.
The next day Moses tried to stop two Hebrews from fighting, asking the one in the wrong why he struck his neighbor.
The man rejected Moses: “Who made you ruler over us?” His secret was out, and Moses was afraid. Israel’s rejection of their deliverer foreshadows later rejections, even of Christ.

f.w: Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?

chapters.n: Pharaoh sought to kill Moses, so he fled to Midian, east of Egypt, and sat down by a well—a classic setting for meeting a future wife in Genesis.

f.g: desert region around the Gulf of Aqaba

chapters.n: The priest of Midian had seven daughters who came to water their father’s flock.
Rough shepherds drove the women away, but Moses stood up for them and watered their flock—again defending the oppressed.

f.g: Hebrew “saved them,” the word for deliverance

chapters.n: Their father Reuel—also called Jethro—asked why they came home so early.
They described their rescuer as an Egyptian—Moses still looked and dressed like one.
Reuel scolded them for leaving the man behind and invited him to a meal—hospitality was a sacred duty.
Moses agreed to stay, and Reuel gave him his daughter Zipporah as a wife. Moses spent about forty years in Midian.
Moses named his son Gershom, meaning roughly “a stranger there,” because he felt like a foreigner in a foreign land.

f.g: sounds like ger sham, “a stranger there”

chapters.n: Years later the king of Egypt died, but the slavery continued. Israel groaned and cried out, and their cry rose to God.

f.w: their cry came up unto God

chapters.n: God heard and remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. “Remembered” means God was about to act on His promises.
God saw Israel and took notice of them. The chapter ends with God turning toward His people—setting up the burning bush.
Once a prince of Egypt, Moses now tends his father-in-law’s sheep. He leads the flock deep into the wilderness to Horeb, the “mountain of God,” also called Sinai.

f.g: Moses received the priesthood from Jethro, according to latter-day revelation.

chapters.n: The Lord appeared in a flame of fire in a bush that burned but did not burn up. Fire often signals God’s holy presence. The Joseph Smith Translation reads “the presence of the Lord” rather than an angel.
Curious, Moses decided to step aside and look closer. Revelation often begins when we turn aside to notice what God is showing us.
When the Lord saw Moses turn to look, He called his name twice. Moses answered, “Here am I”—ready to listen.
God tells Moses to keep his distance and remove his sandals, because God’s presence makes the ground holy. Removing shoes showed reverence and humility.
God identifies Himself as the God of Moses’s ancestors—the covenant God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses hid his face in awe.

f.w: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob

chapters.n: The Lord says He has seen His people’s misery, heard their cries, and knows their sorrows. God is not distant from human suffering.
God has “come down” to rescue Israel and bring them to a good, spacious land “flowing with milk and honey”—rich pasture and plenty. The land was then home to many Canaanite peoples.

f.w: I am come down to deliver them

f.g: a land of rich pasture and abundance

chapters.n: God repeats that their cry has reached Him and He has seen the cruelty of Egypt.
Then the call: “I will send thee.” God answers Israel’s prayers by sending a person—Moses—to act.

f.w: I will send thee unto Pharaoh

chapters.n: Moses replies, “Who am I?” Once confident in his own strength, he now feels inadequate—a humility that makes him teachable.
God’s answer is not about who Moses is, but who God is: “I will be with thee.” The sign will be Israel worshipping God on this very mountain.

f.w: Certainly I will be with thee

chapters.n: Moses asks what name to give when the people ask who sent him. In the ancient world a name revealed someone’s nature.

God reveals His name: “I AM THAT I AM”—the self-existent, eternal One. Jesus later applied “I am” to Himself, and Latter-day Saints understand the God speaking here to be Jehovah, the premortal Christ.

f.g: Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh — “I am who I am” or “I will be what I will be.”

chapters.n: God gives His covenant name, YHWH (“the LORD,” Jehovah), related to “I AM.” This will be His name forever, remembered by every generation.

f.g: YHWH (Jehovah), from the Hebrew verb “to be”
the name by which I am to be remembered

chapters.n: Moses is to gather Israel’s elders and tell them God has “visited” them—the very word Joseph used when he promised God would deliver them.
God repeats the promise: He will bring them out of affliction into a land of plenty.
The elders will listen. Together they will ask Pharaoh to let Israel take a three-day journey to worship God—a modest first request that tests Pharaoh’s heart.
God warns Moses that Pharaoh will refuse unless compelled by a mighty hand.
God will stretch out His hand and strike Egypt with wonders—the plagues—and then Pharaoh will let them go.
God will give Israel favor with the Egyptians so they will not leave empty-handed, as God had promised Abraham.
Israelite women will ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver, gold, and clothing. After centuries of unpaid labor, it was like back wages. Some of this would later be given for the tabernacle.

f.g: ask for, request (not borrow intending to return)

chapters.n: Moses raises another objection: What if the people don’t believe the Lord appeared to me?
God asks a simple question: “What is that in thine hand?” God works with what Moses already has—an ordinary shepherd’s staff.
When Moses threw the staff down, it became a snake, and Moses ran from it. In Egypt the cobra was a symbol of Pharaoh’s power.
God told Moses to grab it by the tail—the dangerous way to hold a snake. When he obeyed, it became a staff again. Faith means acting even when afraid.
This sign would help the people believe the God of their fathers had truly appeared to Moses.
For a second sign, Moses’s hand turned white with a skin disease when he put it inside his cloak.

f.g: the fold of his garment at the chest
diseased with a skin condition, white and flaky; not necessarily modern leprosy

chapters.n: When he put it in again, his hand was healed. God has power both to afflict and to heal.
If the first sign did not convince the people, the second would.
A third sign: water from the Nile poured on dry ground would turn to blood—a preview of the first plague.
Moses objects again: he is not a skilled speaker, “slow of speech.” Many prophets have felt inadequate to speak for God.
God responds: Who made the human mouth? The One who made Moses can help him speak.
God promises to be with Moses’s mouth and teach him what to say—a promise He makes to His servants still.

f.w: I will be with thy mouth

chapters.n: Moses finally pleads: “Please send someone else.” This was no longer humility, but reluctance.
The Lord was displeased, yet still provided help: Moses’s older brother Aaron, a fluent speaker, was already on his way to meet him.

f.w: the anger of the LORD was kindled

chapters.n: Moses would give Aaron the words, and God would teach them both.
Aaron would be Moses’s spokesman, and Moses would be “as God” to Aaron—the source of the message, the way God is to a prophet.

f.w: thou shalt be to him instead of God

chapters.n: Moses was to take the staff to work signs. The ordinary rod is now “the rod of God.”
Moses respectfully asked his father-in-law’s permission to return to Egypt, and Jethro sent him with a blessing of peace.
The Lord reassured Moses that those who wanted to kill him were dead—echoed later when the angel tells Joseph to return from Egypt with Jesus.

f.w: all the men are dead which sought thy life

chapters.n: Moses set out for Egypt with his family, carrying the “rod of God.”
God warns that Pharaoh will resist. The KJV says God will harden Pharaoh’s heart; the Joseph Smith Translation says Pharaoh will harden his own heart, preserving his agency.
Moses is to tell Pharaoh that Israel is God’s “firstborn son”—a relationship of love, privilege, and responsibility.

f.w: Israel is my son, even my firstborn

chapters.n: Because Pharaoh will refuse to free God’s firstborn, God warns that Pharaoh’s own firstborn will die. This foreshadows the final plague.

f.w: I will slay thy son, even thy firstborn

chapters.n: A mysterious episode: on the way, the Lord was ready to take Moses’s life. The JST explains the Lord was angry because Moses had not circumcised his son, neglecting the covenant sign.

f.g: a lodging place for the night
JST says the Lord was angry with Moses “because he had not circumcised his son.”

chapters.n: Zipporah quickly circumcised their son with a flint knife and touched Moses’s feet with it. Her words, “a bloody husband,” are difficult; she may be noting the blood that saved Moses.
The Lord let Moses go. Before leading Israel in covenant, Moses had to keep the covenant in his own home.
The Lord sent Aaron to meet Moses at the mountain of God, and the brothers greeted each other with a kiss.
Moses told Aaron everything the Lord had said and the signs he was to perform.
Together they gathered Israel’s elders, just as God had instructed.
Aaron spoke for Moses and performed the signs before the people.
The people believed. Hearing that God had seen their suffering, they bowed and worshipped. Moses’s fears were unfounded.
Moses and Aaron deliver God’s message to Pharaoh: “Let my people go,” so they can worship Him in the wilderness. This famous demand begins the contest between the Lord and Pharaoh.
Pharaoh, who considered himself a god, scoffs: “Who is the LORD?” The plagues will answer his question.
Moses and Aaron restate the request politely, asking for a three-day trip to sacrifice so that God will not punish Israel for neglecting Him.
Pharaoh accuses them of distracting the workers and orders everyone back to work.

f.w: let the people from their works
f.g: keep the people from their work

chapters.n: Pharaoh complains that with so many laborers, Moses is causing costly downtime.
That same day Pharaoh gave orders to the Egyptian slave drivers and the Israelite foremen.
Straw, mixed into mud to strengthen bricks, would no longer be supplied; the Israelites had to gather it themselves.

f.g: chopped straw, used as a binder in mud bricks

chapters.n: Yet they had to produce the same number of bricks. Pharaoh dismissed their desire to worship as laziness.
Pharaoh’s strategy: crush them with work so they won’t listen to “empty words” of deliverance.
The order was announced to the people: no more straw from Pharaoh.
Find your own straw—but not one brick less.
The people spread throughout Egypt gathering stubble—the leftover stalks in harvested fields.

f.g: short stalks left in a field after harvest

chapters.n: The slave drivers kept pushing them to meet the daily quota.
The Israelite foremen were beaten when the quotas weren’t met.
The foremen appealed directly to Pharaoh, asking why he was treating his servants this way.
They protested that the demand was impossible and the fault lay with Pharaoh’s own people.
Pharaoh repeated his accusation: “You are lazy!” Hard hearts often explain away the pleas of others.
He sent them back to work with the same impossible quota.
The foremen realized they were in serious trouble.
Leaving Pharaoh, they found Moses and Aaron waiting for them.
They blamed Moses and Aaron for making them hateful to Pharaoh—“a stench” in his eyes—and putting a sword in Egypt’s hand.

f.w: made our savour to be abhorred
f.g: made us stink, made us repulsive

chapters.n: Moses took his anguish to the Lord in honest prayer: Why have you let this happen? Why did you send me? Scripture allows such raw prayers.
Since Moses came, things had only gotten worse, and deliverance had not come. Often the darkest moment comes just before God’s intervention.

f.w: neither hast thou delivered thy people at all

chapters.n: The Lord answers Moses’s complaint: “Now you will see.” Pharaoh will not only let Israel go—he will drive them out.
God begins with a solemn declaration: “I am the LORD”—Jehovah. The same phrase frames this whole speech.
The KJV suggests the patriarchs did not know the name Jehovah. The Joseph Smith Translation changes this to a question—“was not my name known unto them?”—affirming they did know it.

f.g: JST makes this a question showing the patriarchs knew the name.

chapters.n: God reminds Moses of His covenant to give Canaan to the patriarchs, where they lived as foreigners.

f.g: the land where they lived as sojourners

chapters.n: God has heard Israel’s groaning and remembered His covenant.
God makes promises in a series of “I will”s: I will bring you out, rescue you, and redeem you. To “redeem” means to buy back or free a relative—a word central to Christ’s work.

f.g: Hebrew ga’al — to act as a family redeemer, buying back a relative
a sign of God’s power in action

chapters.n: “I will take you to me for a people, and I will be to you a God”—the heart of the covenant relationship, repeated throughout scripture.

f.w: I will take you to me for a people

chapters.n: God will bring them into the land promised to their fathers as an inheritance. Jewish Passover tradition uses the four promises of verses 6–7 for its four cups of wine.
Moses repeated these promises, but the people were too crushed in spirit to listen.
The Lord speaks to Moses again.
God sends Moses back to Pharaoh to demand Israel’s release.
Moses protests: if Israel won’t listen, why would Pharaoh? He calls himself one of “uncircumcised lips”—that is, an unskilled speaker.

f.g: lips that are “closed” or unfit; poor at speaking

chapters.n: God gave Moses and Aaron a formal commission to Israel and to Pharaoh.
The story pauses for a genealogy that shows who Moses and Aaron are. It begins with Reuben’s clans.

f.w: the heads of their fathers' houses

chapters.n: Simeon’s clans come next, matching the list in Genesis.
The list then focuses on Levi, the tribe of Moses and Aaron. Levi lived 137 years.
Gershon’s sons are named; their descendants later cared for the tabernacle’s curtains.
Kohath’s sons include Amram, father of Moses. Kohath lived 133 years.
Merari’s sons complete the main Levite families, who later carried the tabernacle frame.
Amram married Jochebed, his aunt (later forbidden by the law of Moses), and they had Aaron and Moses. Miriam is not listed here.

f.g: a name likely meaning “Jehovah is glory”

chapters.n: Izhar’s sons include Korah, who will later rebel against Moses and Aaron.
Uzziel’s sons include Mishael and Elzaphan, who later carried out the bodies of Nadab and Abihu.
Aaron married Elisheba from the leading family of Judah. Their four sons became priests; Nadab and Abihu would die for offering unauthorized fire.

f.g: “God is an oath”; Elizabeth is the Greek form

chapters.n: Korah’s sons are named; though Korah perished, his descendants survived and later wrote several Psalms.
Eleazar, Aaron’s son, fathered Phinehas, who would become known for his zeal for the Lord. These are the leading priestly families.
The genealogy’s point: this is the same Aaron and Moses whom the Lord commanded to lead Israel out “by their armies”—organized like hosts.

f.g: by their divisions, in organized companies

chapters.n: These ordinary men from Levi’s line are the ones who confronted the king of Egypt.
The story picks up again where it left off before the genealogy.
The Lord repeats His command: speak to Pharaoh everything I tell you.
Moses repeats his worry about his poor speech, which the next chapter answers.

f.w: how shall Pharaoh hearken unto me

chapters.n: God answers Moses’s fear: Moses will be “as God” to Pharaoh—speaking with divine authority—and Aaron will be his prophet, his spokesman.

f.w: I have made thee a god to Pharaoh
f.g: You will stand in God’s place, with His authority.
spokesman, one who speaks for another

chapters.n: Moses will speak God’s words to Aaron, and Aaron will speak them to Pharaoh.
God foretells that Pharaoh’s heart will harden. The Joseph Smith Translation consistently renders these passages as Pharaoh hardening his own heart—Pharaoh chose to resist.
Pharaoh’s refusal will lead God to act with great judgments and bring His people out like an organized army.

f.g: Israel, organized as the Lord’s hosts

chapters.n: The purpose of the plagues: Egypt will come to know that Jehovah is the Lord—the true God above Egypt’s gods.

f.w: the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD

chapters.n: Moses and Aaron obeyed exactly. The repeated phrase stresses complete obedience.
Moses was eighty and Aaron eighty-three. God called them to their greatest work in old age; it is never too late to serve.
The Lord gives Moses and Aaron instructions for their next meeting with Pharaoh.
If Pharaoh demanded a miracle as proof, Aaron was to throw down his staff to become a serpent.

f.g: Hebrew tannin — a large serpent or crocodile-like creature

chapters.n: Aaron threw down his staff before Pharaoh and his court, and it became a serpent.
Pharaoh summoned his wise men and sorcerers, who imitated the sign by their secret arts. Paul names two of them, Jannes and Jambres.
Their staffs also became serpents, but Aaron’s staff swallowed theirs—a clear sign that God’s power overpowers false power.

f.w: Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods

chapters.n: Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he refused to listen, just as the Lord had foretold.
The Lord tells Moses that Pharaoh’s heart is “heavy” or stubborn; he refuses to release the people.

f.g: Here the Hebrew is kaved, “heavy, unresponsive.”

chapters.n: Moses is to meet Pharaoh at the Nile in the morning, staff in hand. Pharaoh may have gone to the river for religious rites—the Nile was worshipped as a source of life.

f.g: to meet him when he comes

chapters.n: Moses must remind Pharaoh that the God of the Hebrews has demanded Israel’s release, and so far Pharaoh has not listened.
The first plague is announced: the Nile’s water will turn to blood. The life-giving river, worshipped by Egypt, will become a source of death.

f.w: they shall be turned to blood

chapters.n: The fish would die and the river stink, making the water undrinkable.
Every water source in Egypt would be affected—streams, canals, ponds, even water stored in wooden and stone containers.
Aaron struck the Nile before Pharaoh, and the water turned to blood.
The fish died, the river stank, and blood was everywhere in Egypt.
Pharaoh’s magicians imitated the sign on a small scale, so Pharaoh hardened his heart. Notice they could worsen the problem but not fix it.
Pharaoh simply went home and refused to take it to heart. Ignoring God’s signs is one way hearts harden.

f.w: neither did he set his heart to this
f.g: he paid no attention to it

chapters.n: The Egyptians had to dig wells near the river to find drinkable water.
The plague lasted seven full days.
The Lord sends Moses again with the same demand: Let my people go, that they may serve me. The goal is not just freedom, but worship.
If Pharaoh refuses, the second plague will strike: frogs throughout the land.
Frogs will swarm out of the Nile into houses, bedrooms, beds, ovens, and bread bowls. Egyptians associated frogs with a fertility goddess, Heqet—now the symbol becomes a nuisance.
The frogs will climb on Pharaoh himself, his people, and his officials—no one would escape.
Aaron is told to stretch his staff over the waters to bring up the frogs.
Aaron obeyed, and frogs covered Egypt.
The magicians produced frogs too—adding to the problem rather than solving it.
For the first time, Pharaoh asks Moses to pray to the Lord for relief, promising to let Israel go.
Moses courteously lets Pharaoh set the time for the frogs to leave, so the timing itself will prove the Lord’s power.

f.g: “I give you the honor” — you choose the time

chapters.n: Pharaoh says “tomorrow”—oddly willing to endure one more night of frogs. Moses agrees, so Pharaoh will know no one is like the Lord.

f.w: there is none like unto the LORD our God

chapters.n: Moses promises the frogs will leave and stay in the river.
Moses prayed earnestly to the Lord about the frogs.
The Lord answered Moses’s prayer: the frogs died in houses, courtyards, and fields.
Piled in heaps, the dead frogs made the land stink.
As soon as relief came, Pharaoh hardened his heart again. Promises made in crisis are often forgotten when the pressure lifts.
Without warning, the third plague comes: Aaron strikes the dust, and it becomes gnats or lice.

f.g: Hebrew kinnim — gnats, lice, or mosquitoes

chapters.n: Aaron struck the ground, and swarms of insects covered people and animals across Egypt.
This time the magicians failed. They could not copy the miracle.
The magicians admitted, “This is the finger of God.” Even so, Pharaoh would not listen. Jesus later used the same phrase about His power over evil.
The Lord sends Moses to meet Pharaoh at the river in the early morning with the familiar demand.
The fourth plague is threatened: swarms of flies filling houses and covering the ground.

f.g: Hebrew ‘arov — swarms, perhaps of biting flies or mixed insects

chapters.n: For the first time, God will make a distinction: no flies in Goshen, where Israel lived. This shows the plagues are not random but come from the Lord.

f.w: I am the LORD in the midst of the earth
f.g: The Lord rules even in Egypt, not just in Israel.

chapters.n: God will mark a clear difference between His people and Pharaoh’s people—a sign that would come tomorrow.
Dense swarms filled Egypt, ruining the land, while Goshen was spared.
Pharaoh offers a compromise: sacrifice to your God—but here in Egypt.
Moses refuses. Israel’s animal sacrifices would offend Egyptians, some of whom regarded certain animals as sacred, and could provoke violence.

f.g: something Egyptians considered detestable or taboo

chapters.n: Moses insists on the full request: three days into the wilderness, as God commands. There is no partial obedience.
Pharaoh agrees, but “not very far”—and asks Moses to pray for him.
Moses agrees to pray for the flies to leave tomorrow, but warns Pharaoh not to deceive them again.
Moses left and prayed to the Lord.
The Lord removed every fly—not one remained.
But Pharaoh hardened his heart again and would not let Israel go. The cycle of plea and broken promise continues.
Moses is sent once more to Pharaoh with the Lord’s unchanging demand.
God warns Pharaoh what will happen if he keeps holding Israel.
The fifth plague: a deadly disease on Egypt’s livestock in the fields. Egypt revered certain animals, like the bull, as sacred.

f.g: a deadly animal disease, a cattle plague

chapters.n: Again God will make a distinction: not one of Israel’s animals will die.
The Lord set a time—tomorrow—so the timing would prove the plague came from Him.
The next day the Egyptian livestock in the fields died, but not one Israelite animal.

f.g: all the livestock in the fields (some survived, as verse 19 shows)

chapters.n: Pharaoh even sent officials to verify that Israel’s animals were untouched—yet he remained stubborn. Evidence alone does not change a hard heart.
The sixth plague comes without warning. Moses throws furnace soot into the air—perhaps soot from the very kilns where Israelite slaves made bricks.
The dust would cause festering boils on people and animals.
Moses did as instructed, and boils broke out across Egypt.
The magicians couldn’t even stand before Moses, because they were covered in boils themselves. Their defeat is complete.
For the first time, the text says the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart. The JST reads that Pharaoh hardened his own heart. Either way, Pharaoh had repeatedly chosen resistance.

f.w: the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh

chapters.n: Moses is sent early in the morning with the demand again.
God warns that the full force of His plagues is coming, so Pharaoh will know there is no god like Him.
God could already have wiped Pharaoh out with disease.
Instead, God has allowed Pharaoh to remain so that God’s power and name would be known throughout the earth. Paul quotes this verse.

f.w: for this cause have I raised thee up

chapters.n: God asks: Are you still lifting yourself up against my people?

f.g: set yourself up proudly; act as a barrier

chapters.n: The seventh plague: the worst hailstorm in Egypt’s history, coming tomorrow. Hail was very rare in Egypt.
Even in judgment, God offers mercy: bring your animals and servants inside and they will live.
Some of Pharaoh’s officials feared the Lord’s word and sheltered their servants and animals—Egyptians, too, could choose to believe.

f.w: He that feared the word of the LORD

chapters.n: Others ignored the warning and left theirs in the fields.
The Lord tells Moses to stretch out his hand to the sky to bring the hail.
Thunder and hail fell, and lightning (“fire”) ran along the ground.

f.w: the fire ran along upon the ground

chapters.n: It was the worst storm Egypt had ever known—hail mixed with lightning.
The hail struck people, animals, plants, and broke trees all over Egypt.
But Goshen, where Israel lived, had no hail.
Pharaoh admits, “I have sinned… the LORD is righteous.” His words sound like repentance, but his actions will show it was only fear.
Pharaoh pleads for the thunder and hail to stop and promises to let Israel go immediately.
Moses agrees to pray once outside the city, so Pharaoh will know the earth belongs to the Lord, not to Egypt’s gods.
Yet Moses sees through him: you still do not truly fear the Lord.
The flax and barley, which were ripe, were ruined. Flax was used for linen; barley for bread and beer.
Wheat and spelt ripen later, so they survived—leaving something for the locusts to come.
Moses left the city, prayed, and the storm stopped.
Once the storm ceased, Pharaoh “sinned yet more” and hardened his heart, along with his officials.
Pharaoh still refused, just as the Lord had foretold through Moses.
The Lord sends Moses back to Pharaoh, explaining that these signs are meant to reveal God’s power. The JST again reads that Pharaoh had hardened his own heart.
The plagues were also for future generations: parents would tell their children and grandchildren what the Lord did. This is why Passover retells the story every year.

f.w: tell in the ears of thy son

chapters.n: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh, “How long will you refuse to humble yourself?” Humility is the real issue.
If Pharaoh refuses, locusts will invade tomorrow.
The locusts will be so many that the ground can’t be seen. They will devour whatever the hail left.
They will fill every house in a swarm unlike anything seen before. Then Moses simply turned and left.
Pharaoh’s own officials begged him to give in: Don’t you realize Egypt is ruined? Even his advisers saw what he would not.
Pharaoh called Moses back and agreed—but asked exactly who would go.
Moses insisted: everyone—young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds. Worship of the Lord involves the whole family.

f.w: with our young and with our old

chapters.n: Pharaoh answered sarcastically and threateningly: “The Lord be with you if I let your children go!” He suspected they would never return.

f.g: you are plotting evil; or, trouble awaits you

chapters.n: Pharaoh would let only the men go, keeping the families as hostages. Then he had Moses and Aaron thrown out.
The Lord tells Moses to stretch out his hand to bring the locusts.
An east wind blew all day and night, and by morning it had carried in the locusts. God uses natural forces to accomplish His purposes.
The locusts swarmed throughout Egypt in unmatched numbers.
They covered the land so thickly it turned dark. Not a green plant was left anywhere.
Pharaoh hurriedly summoned Moses and Aaron and confessed sin against the Lord and against them.
He pleaded for forgiveness “only this once” and called the locusts “this death.”
Moses left and prayed for Pharaoh.
The Lord sent a strong west wind that swept every locust into the Red Sea.
Yet Pharaoh’s heart remained hard, and he did not let Israel go.
The ninth plague comes without warning: a darkness so thick it could be felt. Egypt’s chief god was the sun god, Ra—now even the sun is hidden.
Moses raised his hand, and thick darkness covered Egypt for three days.

f.g: Compare the three days of darkness in the Americas at Christ’s death.

chapters.n: People couldn’t see each other or move for three days—but the Israelites had light where they lived. God’s people have light even when the world is in darkness.

f.w: all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings

chapters.n: Pharaoh offers another compromise: the families may go, but the livestock must stay.
Moses refuses: they need animals for sacrifices and offerings to the Lord.

chapters.n: Not a single hoof would be left behind, because they did not yet know what the Lord would require. Full obedience allows no partial terms.

f.w: there shall not an hoof be left behind

chapters.n: Pharaoh’s heart was hardened again, and he would not let them go.
Furious, Pharaoh ordered Moses out and threatened him with death if he ever came back.
Moses agreed: “I will see your face no more.” The time for negotiation was over.
The Lord tells Moses one final plague remains. After it, Pharaoh will not just permit Israel to leave—he will drive them out completely.
Moses is to tell the Israelites to ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver and gold, as God had promised at the burning bush.
God gave Israel favor with the Egyptians, and Moses himself was now highly respected by Pharaoh’s officials and the people.
Moses announces the Lord’s words: about midnight, the Lord Himself will go out through Egypt.
Every firstborn in Egypt would die, from Pharaoh’s heir to the lowest servant grinding grain, and even the firstborn of animals. Pharaoh had killed Israel’s sons; now judgment falls on his own.

f.w: all the firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die

f.g: at the hand-mill—the humblest job of grinding grain

chapters.n: A loud wail of grief would rise from all Egypt, unlike any before or after.
But among Israel, not even a dog would growl—a picture of total calm and safety. The Lord makes a clear distinction between His people and Egypt.

f.w: shall not a dog move his tongue
f.g: there will be complete peace; not even a dog will bark

chapters.n: Moses predicts Pharaoh’s officials will bow before him begging Israel to leave. Then Moses left Pharaoh in hot anger.
The Lord reminds Moses that Pharaoh will not listen, so that God’s wonders will be multiplied.
A summary of the plague narrative: Moses and Aaron did all these wonders, yet Pharaoh’s heart stayed hard. The JST reads “Pharaoh hardened his heart.”
While still in Egypt, the Lord gives Moses and Aaron instructions for the Passover—the defining ordinance of Israel’s faith.
This month (later called Abib or Nisan, in spring) would begin Israel’s religious year. Their freedom marked a new beginning, as if time itself started over.
On the tenth day, each household was to select a lamb—one lamb per family.
Small households should share a lamb with neighbors so none would go to waste.
The lamb had to be flawless, a year-old male. Christ is called a lamb “without blemish and without spot.”
The lamb was kept until the fourteenth day and then killed at twilight by all Israel. Jesus was crucified at Passover time.
Blood was smeared on the doorposts and the top of the door frame of each house. The blood marked who was under the Lord’s protection.

f.g: the lintel, the beam over the door

chapters.n: They ate the lamb roasted, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs—bitterness recalling slavery, and bread made in haste.

f.g: bread made without yeast, flat bread

chapters.n: The lamb was not to be eaten raw or boiled, but roasted whole, including head, legs, and inner parts.
Nothing could be left until morning; leftovers were burned. The sacrifice was complete and holy.
They were to eat dressed for travel—belts fastened, sandals on, staff in hand—ready to leave at once. It is “the LORD’s passover.”

f.g: long robes tucked into the belt for travel

chapters.n: That night the Lord would strike Egypt’s firstborn and judge Egypt’s gods—proving they were powerless.

chapters.n: “When I see the blood, I will pass over you.” The blood was the sign of safety. Latter-day Saints and other Christians see the lamb’s blood as pointing to Christ, “our passover,” whose blood saves.

chapters.n: Passover would be a permanent memorial feast, kept every year for all generations.

chapters.n: For seven days they would eat only unleavened bread and remove all yeast from their homes. Leaven later became a symbol of sin and corruption.
The first and seventh days were sacred assemblies, with no work except preparing food.
The Feast of Unleavened Bread commemorates the very day God brought Israel out of Egypt.
The dates are fixed: from the evening of the fourteenth to the evening of the twenty-first.
No yeast was to be found in any home for seven days—a rule for both native Israelites and foreigners living among them.
A summary: eat nothing leavened, wherever you live.
Moses passes the instructions on to Israel’s elders: choose lambs and kill the Passover.
Using hyssop, a bushy plant, they were to paint the blood on the doorframe and stay inside until morning.

f.g: a small aromatic plant used like a brush for sprinkling

chapters.n: When the Lord sees the blood, He will pass over and not allow the destroyer to enter. Latter-day revelation promises the destroying angel will pass by the obedient.
This ordinance would be kept forever by Israel and their children.
They were to continue observing Passover when they entered the promised land.
Children would naturally ask, “What does this ceremony mean?” God built teaching moments into worship.

f.w: What mean ye by this service?

chapters.n: Parents would answer: it is the Lord’s Passover, who spared our homes. The people bowed and worshipped.
Israel did exactly as the Lord commanded. Their obedience is what saved them.
At midnight the Lord struck every firstborn in Egypt—from Pharaoh’s palace to the prison.

f.w: the captive that was in the dungeon

chapters.n: Pharaoh and all Egypt rose in the night with loud wailing; every home had someone dead. Pharaoh learns the cost of resisting God.
That very night Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron—though he had vowed never to see Moses again—and ordered Israel to go and worship the Lord.

f.w: Rise up, and get you forth

chapters.n: He even told them to take their flocks and herds—every condition granted—and asked Moses to bless him.
The Egyptians urged them to hurry, fearing they would all die.
The Israelites took their unrisen dough in kneading bowls wrapped in their cloaks on their shoulders.
Following Moses’s instruction, they asked the Egyptians for silver, gold, and clothing.
The Lord made the Egyptians willing to give. Israel left with the wealth of Egypt, just as God had promised Abraham.

Israel traveled from Rameses to Succoth—about 600,000 men on foot, plus women and children. Scholars debate how to read these large numbers, but the point is clear: a small family had become a great people.

f.g: “booths,” a place in the eastern Delta

chapters.n: A “mixed multitude” of non-Israelites went with them—perhaps Egyptians and others who had come to believe in Israel’s God.
They baked flat cakes from the unrisen dough, because they had to leave so quickly. This is why unleavened bread is eaten at Passover.
Israel’s stay in Egypt totaled 430 years. (Greek and Samaritan versions count the patriarchs’ time in Canaan too.)
On exactly that day, all the Lord’s “hosts” left Egypt—God keeps His appointed times.
This night is to be specially observed by Israel for all generations—a night of watching to the Lord.

f.g: a night of vigil, of watching

chapters.n: The Lord gives rules for who may eat the Passover: no uncommitted foreigner.
A purchased servant may eat it once circumcised—brought into the covenant.
Temporary foreign residents and hired workers who were not in the covenant could not eat it.
It must be eaten in one house, and none of the lamb’s bones broken. John notes that none of Jesus’s bones were broken on the cross.

f.w: neither shall ye break a bone thereof

chapters.n: The whole community of Israel must keep the Passover.
A foreigner who wanted to keep the Passover could join fully by circumcision and then be treated as native-born. The covenant was open to all who would enter it.

f.w: he shall be as one that is born in the land

chapters.n: One law applies to the native and the foreigner alike—equal standing under the covenant.
All Israel obeyed as the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron.
That very day the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, organized by their tribes. The great Exodus had begun.
Right after the Exodus, the Lord gives Moses instructions about Israel’s firstborn.
Every firstborn male, human and animal, belongs to the Lord. Having spared Israel’s firstborn, God claims them as His own.
Moses tells the people to remember this day of release from “the house of bondage,” accomplished by the Lord’s mighty hand.
They left in the month of Abib, meaning “fresh ears of grain”—springtime.

f.g: “young ears of grain”; later called Nisan

chapters.n: Once in the promised land, they must keep this observance every year in this month.
Seven days of unleavened bread end with a festival on the seventh day.
No yeast was to be seen anywhere in their territory during the feast.
Parents were to explain to their children: we do this because of what the Lord did for me. Each generation was to see the Exodus as personal.

chapters.n: The feast would serve as a reminder, as if on their hand and forehead, keeping God’s law in their mouths. Later Jews literally wore small scripture boxes (tefillin) based on verses like this.

chapters.n: This ordinance must be kept at its appointed time every year.
When the Lord gives them Canaan as promised, they must observe the law of the firstborn.
All firstborn males—of people and livestock—were to be dedicated to the Lord.

f.g: buy back by paying a substitute

chapters.n: When children ask what this means, parents should tell of the Lord’s strong hand in delivering them from slavery.
Because the Lord struck Egypt’s firstborn when Pharaoh refused, Israel offers its firstborn animals and redeems its sons.

chapters.n: This would be a sign on the hand and “frontlets” between the eyes—an ever-present reminder.

Pharaoh prepared his chariot and gathered his army.
He took six hundred elite chariots and all of Egypt’s chariots with officers—the most advanced military power of the day.

f.g: officers (possibly the third man in each chariot)

chapters.n: Pharaoh pursued Israel, who were marching out boldly, “with a high hand”—confident and unafraid.
The Egyptian army caught up with Israel camped by the sea.
Seeing the army approach, Israel was terrified and cried out to the Lord.
Their fear turned to sarcasm against Moses: “Weren’t there enough graves in Egypt?”
They claim they would rather have stayed slaves than die in the desert. Fear makes bondage look safe.
Moses responds with faith: Don’t be afraid. Stand firm and watch the Lord save you. These Egyptians you will never see again.

f.w: stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD

chapters.n: “The LORD shall fight for you.” Their part was to trust and be still.

chapters.n: The Lord tells Moses that now is the time not only to pray but to move: “go forward.” Faith acts.
Moses was to raise his staff over the sea and divide it so Israel could walk through on dry ground.
God would let the Egyptians follow them into the sea and gain glory over Pharaoh’s army.
Then Egypt would know that the Lord is God.
The angel of God and the pillar of cloud moved from the front of Israel to the back, standing between them and the Egyptians like a shield.
The cloud was darkness to Egypt but light to Israel. The same presence of God that blesses the faithful confounds the wicked.

f.w: it was a cloud and darkness to them, but it gave light by night to these

Israel walked through the sea on dry ground with walls of water on both sides. Paul compares this passage to baptism, and Nephi cites it as proof of God’s power.

f.w: went into the midst of the sea upon the dry ground

In the early morning hours, the Lord looked down through the pillar and threw the Egyptian army into confusion.

chapters.n: Chariot wheels jammed or came off, and the Egyptians realized: the Lord is fighting for Israel. Let’s flee!
The Lord tells Moses to stretch out his hand so the waters return on the Egyptians.
At daybreak the sea rushed back. The Egyptians fled straight into it, and the Lord overthrew them.
The waters covered the entire army that had followed Israel—not one survived.
Meanwhile Israel had walked through on dry ground with water walls on either side.
That day the Lord saved Israel, and they saw the Egyptian bodies on the shore. Their oppressors could never enslave them again.

chapters.n: Seeing the Lord’s great power, the people feared Him and believed both the Lord and His servant Moses. Faith in God and trust in His prophet go together.

chapters.n: The Lord is pictured as a warrior who fights for His people. “The LORD is his name”—Jehovah has proven who He is.
Pharaoh’s chariots and best officers were thrown into the sea and drowned.
They sank to the bottom like stones. Poetic repetition drives home the completeness of the victory.
The Lord’s “right hand”—a symbol of strength—shattered the enemy. The repetition is typical Hebrew poetry.
In majesty God overthrew those who rose against Him; His anger burned them up like dry straw.
With a breath from His nostrils—poetic language for the wind—the waters piled up and stood firm like a wall.
The enemy’s boasts are quoted in rapid-fire lines: I will chase, catch, plunder, and destroy. The pride sets up the sudden fall.
One breath from God, and the sea covered them; they sank like lead. Their boasts ended in a moment.
“Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods?” No god of Egypt or any nation compares to Him—majestic in holiness, awesome in praise, working wonders.

The leaders of Edom, Moab, and Canaan—peoples Israel would meet on the way—will be terrified.
Dread will freeze them “as still as a stone” until Israel, the people God “purchased,” passes by into the land.

God will plant Israel on His holy mountain, the place He prepared to dwell—later fulfilled in Jerusalem and the temple on Mount Zion. The word “Sanctuary” is the first mention of a temple-like holy place.
The song climaxes: “The LORD shall reign for ever and ever.” Pharaoh’s reign is ended; God’s never will.

f.w: The LORD shall reign for ever and ever

chapters.n: A prose summary: Pharaoh’s army drowned, but Israel walked through on dry land.
Miriam, called a prophetess, led the women with tambourines and dancing. She is the first woman in the Bible called a prophetess.
Miriam leads the refrain, echoing Moses’s opening line—the women answering in song.
From the sea Moses led Israel into the wilderness of Shur, where for three days they found no water. Joy at the sea quickly gives way to testing.

f.g: the desert between Egypt and Canaan, in the northwest Sinai

chapters.n: At Marah they found water, but it was too bitter to drink. Marah means “bitter.”
The people complained, “What shall we drink?” Murmuring will be a repeated theme in the wilderness.
Moses prayed, and the Lord showed him a piece of wood that made the water sweet. Many see in the tree a symbol of Christ, who makes life’s bitter waters sweet. There God tested Israel.

f.w: the LORD shewed him a tree

chapters.n: God promised: listen and obey, and He would protect them from the diseases of Egypt. “I am the LORD that healeth thee”—Jehovah Rapha.

f.w: I am the LORD that healeth thee

chapters.n: Next they came to Elim, an oasis with twelve springs and seventy palm trees—a place of rest. The numbers echo the twelve tribes and the seventy who went down to Egypt.
A month after leaving Egypt, Israel moved from Elim into the wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Mount Sinai. (“Sin” is a place name, unrelated to the English word.)

f.g: a desert region in the Sinai peninsula

chapters.n: The whole community grumbled against Moses and Aaron. Hardship quickly tested their gratitude.
They romanticized Egypt, remembering pots of meat and plenty of bread, and accused Moses of bringing them out to starve. Memory can make bondage look good.
The Lord answers not with anger but with provision: “I will rain bread from heaven.” They must gather a day’s portion each day—a test of whether they would follow His law.
On the sixth day they would gather and prepare twice as much—providing for the Sabbath.
Moses and Aaron tell the people: by evening you will know it was the Lord who brought you out of Egypt.
In the morning they would see the Lord’s glory. Their complaints, Moses says, are really against the Lord.
God would give meat in the evening and bread in the morning. Moses repeats: “your murmurings are not against us, but against the LORD.”

f.w: your murmurings are not against us, but against the LORD

chapters.n: Moses has Aaron call the people to come before the Lord.
As Aaron spoke, they looked toward the desert and saw the Lord’s glory appear in the cloud.

f.w: the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud

chapters.n: The Lord speaks to Moses.
God has heard their complaints and will provide meat and bread so they will know He is the Lord their God.
That evening quail covered the camp, and in the morning dew lay all around.

f.g: small migratory birds that fly over Sinai in spring

chapters.n: When the dew evaporated, a fine, flaky substance like frost covered the ground.
The people asked, “Man hu?”—“What is it?”—and that question became its name, manna. Moses explained: this is the bread the Lord has given you.

f.g: from Hebrew man hu, “What is it?”

chapters.n: Each person was to gather an omer (about two quarts or two liters) per member of the household.
They gathered, some more and some less.
Miraculously, when measured, everyone had just enough—no surplus and no shortage. Paul uses this as a model for sharing among believers.

f.w: he that gathered much had nothing over

chapters.n: Moses told them not to keep any until morning—they must trust God for tomorrow.
Some disobeyed and kept leftovers; by morning it was full of worms and stank. Moses was angry. Manna could not be hoarded.
Every morning they gathered what they needed, and when the sun grew hot, the rest melted.
On the sixth day they gathered double, and the leaders reported it to Moses.
Moses explained: tomorrow is a holy Sabbath rest. Bake and boil today, and save the rest. This is the first explicit Sabbath command to Israel, before Sinai.

f.w: the rest of the holy sabbath

chapters.n: The Sabbath portion kept overnight did not spoil—a weekly miracle showing God’s hand.
Moses told them to eat it that day, because there would be none in the field on the Sabbath.
Six days to gather; none on the seventh.
Some went out on the Sabbath anyway and found nothing.
The Lord asks: “How long will you refuse to keep my commandments?”
The Sabbath is a gift: God provides a double portion on the sixth day so everyone can rest. Stay home on the seventh day.

f.w: the LORD hath given you the sabbath

chapters.n: So the people rested on the seventh day.
Israel named it manna. It was white like coriander seed and tasted like honey wafers.

chapters.n: The Lord commanded that an omer of manna be preserved for future generations to see how He fed Israel in the wilderness.
Aaron put an omer of manna in a jar to be kept before the Lord. Hebrews says it was kept in the ark of the covenant.
Aaron placed it before “the Testimony”—the tablets of the law later kept in the ark. (This detail is told ahead of time.)

f.g: the tablets of the covenant, kept in the ark

Moses cried to the Lord: “What shall I do?” The people were nearly ready to stone him. Leaders need the Lord’s help too.
The Lord told Moses to go ahead of the people with some elders as witnesses, carrying the same staff that struck the Nile.

f.w: thy rod, wherewith thou smotest the river

Moses named the place Massah (“testing”) and Meribah (“quarreling”), because the people asked, “Is the LORD among us, or not?”—despite His pillar of cloud overhead.
Then Amalek—descendants of Esau—attacked Israel. Deuteronomy says they struck the weak and weary at the rear.
Moses appoints Joshua to lead the fighting while Moses stands on the hill holding the rod of God. This is Joshua’s first appearance.

chapters.n: Joshua fought, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur climbed the hilltop.

Jethro brought Zipporah, Moses’s wife, whom Moses had earlier sent back to her father’s home.

The second son, Eliezer, means “My God is help,” remembering God’s rescue of Moses from Pharaoh’s sword.
Jethro brought the family to Moses at the mountain of God—Sinai.
Jethro sent word ahead that he was arriving with Moses’s family.
Moses went out, bowed respectfully, and kissed his father-in-law. They asked about each other’s welfare and went into the tent—a warm reunion.
Moses told Jethro all the Lord had done to Pharaoh, the hardships of the journey, and how the Lord rescued them. Sharing our experiences of God’s help strengthens others.
Jethro rejoiced at all the good the Lord had done for Israel.
Jethro praised the Lord for delivering Israel from Egypt and Pharaoh.
“Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods”—the very lesson the plagues were meant to teach. Pride was humbled.
Jethro offered sacrifices, and Aaron and Israel’s elders shared a sacred meal with him “before God.”

Jethro said frankly, “What you are doing is not good.” Even a prophet benefits from wise counsel.

Choose capable leaders who fear God, are trustworthy, and hate dishonest gain. Organize them over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
These leaders would judge ordinary matters and bring only major cases to Moses, sharing the load.
If God approves, Moses will be able to endure, and the people will go home in peace. Jethro wisely submits his idea to God’s will.
Moses humbly listened to his father-in-law and did everything he said.
Moses chose capable men and made them leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. Delegation is a pattern in how the Lord’s work is organized.
These leaders judged everyday matters, bringing only difficult cases to Moses.
Moses sent Jethro off, and he returned to his own land.
Exactly two months after leaving Egypt, Israel arrived at the wilderness of Sinai. Here they will stay about a year, receiving the covenant and law.
Coming from Rephidim, they camped in front of the mountain—the same mountain where God first called Moses from the burning bush.
Moses climbed toward God, and the Lord called to him from the mountain with a message for “the house of Jacob.”
God reminds them: You saw what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself. The goal of the Exodus was not just freedom from Egypt, but closeness to God.

f.w: I bare you on eagles' wings

f.g: The Exodus aims at relationship with God.

chapters.n: If Israel truly obeys and keeps His covenant, they will be His “peculiar treasure”—His own special possession—among all peoples.

f.g: Hebrew segullah — a king’s personal treasure, a prized possession

f.w: if ye will obey my voice indeed

chapters.n: Israel was to be “a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation”—a whole people dedicated to God and representing Him to the world. Latter-day Saints see this ideal renewed in covenant and temple blessings.

f.w: a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation

chapters.n: Moses gathered the elders and set before them all the Lord’s words.
The people answered with one voice: “All that the LORD hath spoken we will do.” Moses carried their answer back to the Lord.

f.w: All that the LORD hath spoken we will do

chapters.n: God would come in a thick cloud so the people could hear Him speak with Moses and trust Moses forever.
The people must prepare for two days: sanctify themselves and wash their clothes. Outward cleanliness symbolized inner purity before meeting God.
On the third day the Lord would come down on Mount Sinai in sight of all the people.
Boundaries were set around the mountain. Anyone touching it would die. God’s holiness is real and must be approached on His terms.
A trespasser was to be stoned or shot with arrows—no one should touch the holy ground to retrieve him. When the ram’s horn sounded long, they could approach.
Moses went down, the people consecrated themselves, and washed their clothes.
They were to be ready by the third day and abstain from marital relations during this sacred preparation.

f.g: abstain from sexual relations (as part of ritual preparation)

chapters.n: On the third morning came thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, and a very loud trumpet blast. The whole camp trembled.
Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God; they stood at the foot of the mountain.
Sinai was covered in smoke because the Lord descended in fire. Smoke rose like a furnace, and the whole mountain shook violently.
As the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke and God answered him audibly.
The Lord came down on the summit and called Moses up, and Moses went.
God sent Moses back down to warn the people not to push through to look, lest many die.
Even the priests—probably the firstborn or family heads who offered sacrifices before the Levites were appointed—had to sanctify themselves.

f.g: those who served before the Levitical priesthood was established

chapters.n: Moses replied that the people cannot come up, since the boundaries had been set.

The Lord told Moses to go down and return with Aaron, but not to let the priests or people break through. Latter-day revelation teaches Moses sought to bring Israel into God’s presence, but they hardened their hearts.

f.w: let not the priests and the people break through

chapters.n: Moses went down and spoke to the people, and the next chapter records the Ten Commandments.
God Himself speaks the Ten Commandments aloud to all Israel. These “ten words” are the foundation of the covenant and of much of Western moral law.

f.g: In Hebrew they are called the “Ten Words.”

chapters.n: Before any command, God reminds them who He is and what He has done: I am the Lord who freed you from slavery. Obedience flows from gratitude for deliverance.

f.w: I am the LORD thy God

chapters.n: The first commandment: worship no other gods besides Him. God must come first in our loyalty and love.

f.w: Thou shalt have no other gods before me

chapters.n: The second commandment forbids making idols or carved images to worship—of anything in the sky, on earth, or in the sea.

f.w: Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image

chapters.n: Do not bow down to idols. God is “jealous”—fiercely devoted to His covenant people, like a faithful spouse. Children of those who hate Him often inherit the consequences of their parents’ sins.

f.g: zealous, passionately committed to His covenant people

f.w: visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children
f.g: Children suffer the effects of parents’ sins but are not punished for them.

chapters.n: In contrast, God shows steadfast love to thousands of generations of those who love Him and keep His commandments. Mercy far outweighs judgment.

f.w: them that love me, and keep my commandments

chapters.n: The third commandment: don’t misuse the Lord’s name—whether in empty oaths, profanity, or false claims to speak for Him.
The fourth commandment: remember the Sabbath and keep it holy. “Remember” recalls the manna lesson and the creation.
Work is honored: six days are for labor.
The seventh day belongs to the Lord. No one in the household works—not children, servants, animals, or foreigners. The Sabbath protected the weakest from endless labor.

f.w: thy stranger that is within thy gates

chapters.n: The reason: God made everything in six days and rested on the seventh, then blessed and sanctified that day.
The fifth commandment: honor your father and mother. Paul calls it the first commandment with a promise—long life in the land.

f.w: Honour thy father and thy mother

chapters.n: The sixth commandment forbids murder—the unlawful taking of human life. Jesus extended it to the anger that leads to violence.
The seventh commandment protects marriage: no sexual relations outside it. Jesus extended it to lustful thoughts.
The eighth commandment protects property: do not steal.
The ninth commandment forbids lying about others, especially in court. Justice depends on honest testimony.
The tenth commandment goes to the heart: don’t covet—don’t crave what belongs to others. Sin often begins with desire.

f.g: desire greedily what is not yours

chapters.n: The people saw the thunder, lightning, smoke, and heard the trumpet. Terrified, they backed away and stood at a distance.
They begged Moses to speak to them instead, fearing they would die if God spoke directly. They asked for a mediator.
Moses reassured them: don’t be afraid. God came to test you, so that reverence for Him will keep you from sin. Healthy “fear of God” is awe that guides behavior.
The people stayed far off, while Moses approached the thick darkness where God was. The pattern of a mediator approaching God for the people points to Christ.

f.w: the thick darkness where God was

chapters.n: The Lord tells Moses to remind Israel: you saw that I spoke to you from heaven.
Since they heard God’s voice and saw no form, they must not make gods of silver or gold to stand beside Him.
Israel’s altars were to be simple—made of earth—for burnt offerings and peace offerings. Wherever God causes His name to be remembered, He will come and bless.

f.g: fellowship offerings, partly eaten by the worshipper

f.w: in all places where I record my name

chapters.n: A stone altar must be of uncut stone. Shaping it with tools would profane it—perhaps to avoid carved images or human pride in workmanship.
No steps up to the altar, so priests in robes would not expose themselves—unlike some pagan rituals. Later, priests wore linen undergarments for modesty.
Right after the Ten Commandments, the Lord gives Moses a set of case laws (often called the “Book of the Covenant,” Exodus 21–23) that apply those principles to everyday life in Israel.

f.g: Hebrew mishpatim — rulings or case laws, usually phrased “if… then…”.

chapters.n: A fellow Israelite who sold himself into service to pay a debt could only be held six years. In the seventh year he walked away free, owing nothing — a limit meant to keep poverty from becoming permanent slavery.
The servant leaves in the same family situation he entered. If he came in married, his wife goes free with him; servitude could not be used to break up an existing family.

If the master had given him a wife during his service (likely a servant herself, with a longer term), she and the children remained in the master’s household when he left. This hard case sets up the choice in the next verses.
A servant who loved his family and master could choose to stay permanently rather than leave them behind. The law allowed willing, lifelong service.

f.w: I will not go out free

chapters.n: The choice was made public before the judges, and the servant’s ear was pierced at the doorpost as a sign of lasting belonging to that household. Some see in it an image of willingly listening to and serving one’s master.

f.g: Hebrew ha-elohim, literally “God”; likely means appearing before God at the sanctuary or before judges acting for Him.
A small pointed tool for piercing leather.
For the rest of his life.

chapters.n: A poor father might arrange for his daughter to enter a household as a servant intended for marriage. Her rights differed from a male servant’s because her place involved a future marriage, and the following verses protect her.

f.g: Hebrew amah — here a young woman taken into a household with a view to marriage.

chapters.n: If the master decides not to marry her, he must allow her family to buy her back. He may never sell her to foreigners, because he broke faith with her.

f.g: Bought back, here by her family.

chapters.n: If she is given to the master’s son, she must be treated as a full daughter of the family, not as property.
If he later takes another wife, he still owes the first one food, clothing, and her marital rights. The law guarded a vulnerable woman from being neglected.

f.g: Marital rights, likely including companionship and conjugal relations.

chapters.n: If he fails her in any of these three things, she goes free without any payment. The law gave her a way out of neglect.
Deliberate killing brings the death penalty. This applies the commandment “Thou shalt not kill” and shows how sacred God considers human life.

f.w: shall be surely put to death

chapters.n: Accidental killing is treated differently. God promises a place of refuge where someone who killed by accident could flee and be safe from revenge — later fulfilled in the cities of refuge.

f.w: God deliver him into his hand
f.g: An idiom for an accident not planned by the person.

f.w: a place whither he shall flee

chapters.n: A planned murderer could not hide behind religion: even if he grabbed hold of the altar, he was to be taken away for justice.
Striking a parent was treated as an extremely serious crime, reflecting how strongly the law upheld the commandment to honor father and mother.
Kidnapping a person to sell or keep as a slave was a capital crime. Joseph’s brothers had done just this to him.
Cursing a parent — calling down harm on them or treating them with contempt — was likewise punished by death.
Now the law turns to injuries in a fight that do not kill. Here a man is hurt badly enough to be laid up in bed.
If the injured man recovers enough to walk with a cane, the attacker escapes punishment but must pay for lost work time and medical care until he is fully healed.
Servants were not outside the law’s protection. A master who beat a servant to death was to be punished — a striking protection compared to many ancient law codes.

If the servant survived a day or two, it was presumed the master did not intend to kill, and his financial loss was considered penalty enough. The phrase reflects the ancient setting rather than God’s view of a person’s worth.

f.g: The servant’s labor was the master’s property, so the master bore the loss.

chapters.n: If a pregnant woman is struck during a fight and gives birth early but no lasting harm results, the offender pays a fine set by her husband and confirmed by judges.

f.g: She goes into labor or miscarries; interpreters differ.

chapters.n: If serious harm does follow, the penalty matches the injury, beginning with life for life.
This is the famous “law of retaliation” (lex talionis). Its purpose was to limit punishment to fit the crime — no more than the harm done — and it was applied by judges, not by personal revenge.
The list continues: burns, wounds, and bruises are matched in kind. Jesus later taught His disciples to go beyond this minimum by turning the other cheek.

f.g: A welt or bruise from a blow.

chapters.n: If a master destroys a servant’s eye, the servant goes free as compensation. Even the servant’s body had rights the master could not violate.
Even knocking out a servant’s tooth earns that servant freedom — a strong deterrent against abuse.
An ox that kills a person is stoned and its meat may not be eaten, because it carries bloodguilt. If the owner had no warning, he is not otherwise punished.
But if the ox was known to be dangerous and the owner was warned and did nothing, he shares the guilt for the death — a principle of responsibility for negligence.
The negligent owner could be allowed to pay a ransom instead of dying. This shows the case involved negligence rather than murder, which allowed no ransom.

f.g: A payment to redeem his life.

chapters.n: The same rule applies whether the victim is a child or an adult, son or daughter.
If the ox kills a servant, the owner pays the servant’s master thirty shekels of silver. Strikingly, this was the price paid to betray Jesus.
The law now addresses property damage. Someone who leaves a pit or cistern uncovered is responsible if an animal falls in.

f.g: Likely a cistern dug to store water.

chapters.n: The pit owner must pay the animal’s owner its value, but he keeps the carcass. The goal was fair restitution, not punishment.
When one ox kills another with no prior warning, both owners share the loss equally by dividing the value of the living ox and the dead one.
If the ox was known to be dangerous, its owner must replace the dead ox fully and keep the carcass. Knowing a danger and ignoring it increases responsibility.

A thief who steals and then kills or sells an animal must repay several times over — five oxen for one, four sheep for one. Oxen were worth more because they did farm work, so stealing one did greater harm.
If a burglar is struck and killed while breaking in at night, the homeowner is not guilty of murder, since he could not tell the intruder’s intent in the dark.

f.g: Breaking in, literally “digging through” a mud-brick wall.

f.w: no blood be shed for him
f.g: No bloodguilt falls on the defender.

chapters.n: In daylight things change: the homeowner can see and call for help, so killing the thief becomes bloodguilt. The thief is to repay instead, and if he has nothing he must work off the debt.

f.g: Placed into service to pay what he owes.

chapters.n: If the stolen animal is found alive with the thief, he returns double — the animal plus one more — so stealing always costs more than it gains.
A farmer who lets his animals graze in a neighbor’s field or vineyard must repay with the best produce from his own land. Carelessness toward a neighbor’s livelihood had a price.
Someone who starts a fire that spreads to a neighbor’s grain must pay for the damage. The law teaches responsibility for the unintended results of our actions.

f.g: In the KJV, any grain such as wheat or barley — not American maize.

chapters.n: These verses deal with goods left in someone’s safekeeping. If they are stolen and the thief is caught, the thief pays double.
If no thief is found, the keeper must come before the judges to determine whether he took the goods himself.

f.g: Hebrew ha-elohim, “God” — probably meaning before God at the sanctuary, or before judges acting in His name.

chapters.n: Any disputed property — animals, clothing, or lost items — was to be settled by the judges, and whoever was found in the wrong paid double. Disputes were resolved by law rather than by force.
Now a different case: an animal left in a neighbor’s care dies, is hurt, or is carried off by raiders with no witness.
In such cases the keeper swears an oath before the Lord that he did nothing wrong, and the owner accepts it. Sacred oaths were taken very seriously as a way to settle what no one could prove.

f.g: A solemn oath taken in the Lord’s name.

chapters.n: If the animal was simply stolen from the keeper, he must repay, since he should have guarded it better.
If a wild animal killed it, the keeper brings the remains as proof and owes nothing. Jacob mentions this kind of shepherd’s duty to Laban.
A borrower who damages or loses a borrowed animal while the owner is absent must replace it.
If the owner was present, the borrower is not liable. If the animal was rented, the rental fee covered the risk.

f.g: The fee paid already covered any loss.

chapters.n: A man who seduces an unbetrothed young woman must take responsibility by paying the bride-price and marrying her, protecting her future and standing.
Her father can refuse the marriage, but the man must still pay the full bride-price as if he had married her.

f.g: The customary bride-price paid for an unmarried young woman.

chapters.n: The law now lists offenses against God’s holiness. Sorcery — seeking power from sources other than the Lord — was forbidden because it drew Israel away from Him.

f.g: A sorceress; one who practices magic or occult arts.

chapters.n: Sexual acts with animals, practiced in some surrounding cultures, were a gross perversion of God’s design and carried the death penalty.
Sacrificing to other gods broke the first commandment at its root. Such a person was to be “devoted to destruction.”

f.g: Hebrew ḥerem — devoted or banned, set apart for destruction.

chapters.n: Israel must not mistreat foreigners living among them. Their own memory of being oppressed outsiders in Egypt should make them compassionate.

f.g: A foreign resident living in Israel.

f.w: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt

chapters.n: Widows and orphans, who had no one to defend them in that society, are placed under special protection.
God personally promises to hear the cry of the vulnerable. The weak who have no human defender have a divine one.

f.w: I will surely hear their cry

chapters.n: Those who oppress widows and orphans will themselves suffer the same fate — a vivid warning that God takes cruelty to the helpless personally.
Israelites were not to profit from a poor neighbor’s need. Loans to the poor were to be acts of help, not business.
If a poor man’s cloak was taken as security for a loan, it had to be returned by sunset.
For the poor, that cloak was also their blanket at night. God says He will hear such a person’s cry “for I am gracious” — His own character is the reason for the law.
Israel must not speak contemptuously of God or curse their leaders. Paul quoted this verse when he realized he had spoken sharply to the high priest.

f.g: Hebrew elohim; most read “God,” though some read “judges.”

f.w: curse the ruler of thy people

chapters.n: The first and best of the harvest and the firstborn sons belonged to the Lord. Firstborn sons were redeemed rather than sacrificed, recalling how God spared Israel’s firstborn in Egypt.

f.g: Juices — the first of the wine and oil.

f.w: the firstborn of thy sons shalt thou give unto me

chapters.n: Firstborn animals were also the Lord’s; they stayed with their mother seven days and were offered on the eighth.
Israel is called to be a holy people. Even their diet showed it: they were not to eat meat from an animal killed by wild beasts, which had not been properly drained of blood.
Justice depends on honest testimony. Israelites must not spread false rumors or team up with wrongdoers by testifying falsely in court.

f.g: Spread or accept a false rumor.

chapters.n: Don’t go along with the crowd when the crowd is wrong, and don’t twist your testimony just to side with the majority. Truth is not decided by popular vote.

f.w: follow a multitude to do evil

chapters.n: Fairness cuts both ways: a judge must not favor a poor person simply because he is poor. Justice must be impartial.

f.g: Show favor to, take sides with.

chapters.n: Kindness extends even to enemies. If you find your enemy’s stray animal, return it. Jesus later taught, “Love your enemies.”
If your enemy’s donkey has collapsed under its load, you may feel like walking past — but you must stop and help. Shared work can soften hostility.

f.g: Help him unload and raise the animal.

chapters.n: The poor must not be denied justice in court. Verses 3 and 6 together demand true impartiality.
Stay away from false accusations, and never cause the death of an innocent person. God Himself will not declare the guilty innocent.
Bribes corrupt judgment. A gift can blind even a wise person and make a good person twist his words.
God repeats His command to protect foreigners, appealing to Israel’s own experience: you know how it feels to be an outsider.

f.w: ye know the heart of a stranger

chapters.n: The farmland was to be worked for six years in a row.
Every seventh year the land rested, and whatever grew on its own was left for the poor and for wild animals. This “sabbatical year” taught trust in God and care for the needy.
The weekly Sabbath gave rest not only to the family but to servants, foreigners, and animals. God’s rest was meant for everyone, especially those with the least control over their time.

f.w: on the seventh day thou shalt rest

chapters.n: Be careful to keep all these commands, and don’t even invoke the names of other gods — whether in oaths or prayers.

f.w: make no mention of the name of other gods

chapters.n: Israel was to gather to worship the Lord at three annual festivals.
The first is the Feast of Unleavened Bread, held with Passover in the spring, remembering the Exodus. Worshippers were to bring an offering rather than come empty-handed.

f.g: “Ear of grain” — the spring month later called Nisan (March–April).

chapters.n: The second is the Feast of Harvest (later called Weeks or Pentecost) at the grain harvest; the third is the Feast of Ingathering (Tabernacles or Booths) in the fall when all crops were gathered.

f.g: Also called the Feast of Weeks; in Greek, Pentecost.
Also called the Feast of Tabernacles or Booths.

chapters.n: At these three times every male was to come before the Lord. These pilgrimages bound the nation together in worship.

f.g: Hebrew Adonai YHWH; in the KJV, small-capital GOD represents the divine name.

chapters.n: Sacrificial blood was not to be offered with leavened (yeast) bread, and the fat of the Passover offering was not to be left overnight.
The very first of the harvest belonged to the Lord. The odd command not to boil a young goat in its mother’s milk may reject a pagan ritual or teach respect for the bond between mother and young.

f.w: Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk

chapters.n: God promises to send His Angel to guide and protect Israel all the way to the promised land. He goes before them and prepares their place.

f.g: Hebrew mal’ak — messenger. Here a divine messenger bearing God’s own authority.

f.w: the place which I have prepared

chapters.n: Israel must obey this messenger, because God’s name — His authority and presence — is in him. Many Christians see here the premortal Christ, Jehovah, who leads His people.

f.g: He carries God’s full authority and represents Him.

chapters.n: If Israel obeys, God will fight their battles; their enemies become His enemies.
The Angel will bring them into Canaan, home to many peoples whom God will remove.

f.w: Amorites, and the Hittites, and the Perizzites

chapters.n: Israel must not adopt Canaanite religion but tear down its idols and sacred pillars. The concern was spiritual: false worship would destroy Israel’s covenant.

f.g: Hebrew matsebot — standing stone pillars used in pagan worship.

chapters.n: Serving the Lord brings practical blessings: food and water blessed and sickness removed.
God promises fertility for herds and families and full, long lives for the faithful.

f.w: number of thy days I will fulfil
f.g: You will live out a full lifespan.

chapters.n: God’s reputation would go ahead of Israel, filling their enemies with dread so that they would flee.
God would send “hornets” to drive out the inhabitants — whether literal insects or a figure for panic and terror sent ahead of Israel.
The conquest would not happen all at once, so that the land would not become empty and overrun by wild animals.
