God would drive them out gradually as Israel grew large enough to fill the land. Like many of God’s works, the promise unfolds step by step.
God sets Israel’s ideal borders: from the Red Sea (Gulf of Aqaba) to the Mediterranean, and from the wilderness to the Euphrates. These limits were most nearly reached under David and Solomon.
Israel must not make treaties with the Canaanites or their gods. Covenant loyalty belonged to the Lord alone.
If the Canaanites remained, their worship would trap Israel. The book of Judges later shows this exact warning coming true.
The Lord invites Moses, Aaron, Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu, and seventy elders to come up the mountain to worship — but only at a distance. Each group is given a different level of nearness.
Only Moses, the mediator, may approach the Lord closely. The pattern of graded holiness here anticipates the tabernacle, where only the high priest entered the innermost room.
Moses tells the people everything the Lord has said, and they respond together: “We will do it all.” This is Israel’s first acceptance of the covenant terms.
Moses writes down the Lord’s words, builds an altar, and sets up twelve stone pillars for the twelve tribes — a visible witness that the whole nation is entering the covenant.
Young men offer burnt offerings and peace offerings. Before the formal priesthood of Aaron was set up, chosen men acted for the people.

f.g: Sacrifices wholly burned, symbolizing total dedication.
Fellowship sacrifices partly eaten by the worshippers.

chapters.n: Moses splits the blood in two. Half goes on the altar, representing God’s side of the covenant; the other half is saved for the people.
Moses reads the written covenant aloud, and the people again pledge obedience. Hearing the terms before committing was essential.
Moses sprinkles the rest of the blood on the people, binding both sides in one covenant. Jesus echoed these words at the Last Supper when He spoke of His own blood of the new covenant.

f.w: Behold the blood of the covenant

chapters.n: With the covenant made, the leaders climb the mountain as invited in verse 1.
Astonishingly, they see the God of Israel. Beneath His feet is something like a pavement of brilliant blue stone, clear as the sky itself — language that strains to describe heavenly glory.

f.w: they saw the God of Israel

f.g: Probably lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone.

chapters.n: God did not strike them, though seeing Him was thought fatal. Instead they ate and drank in His presence — a covenant meal celebrating peace with God, an image later fulfilled in the sacrament and the marriage supper of the Lamb.
The Lord calls Moses higher to receive tablets of stone engraved by God Himself, so that he can teach the people.
Moses goes up with his young assistant Joshua, who will later succeed him as Israel’s leader.
Moses leaves Aaron and Hur in charge of the camp while he is away — an arrangement that will be sorely tested in chapter 32.
As Moses climbs, a cloud covers the mountain, the familiar sign of God’s hidden presence.
Moses waits six days at the edge of God’s glory before being called on the seventh. Approaching God often requires patient preparation.

f.g: Hebrew kabod — weight, splendor; the visible radiance of God’s presence.

chapters.n: From the camp below, God’s glory looked like a consuming fire blazing on the summit.
Moses enters the cloud and stays forty days and nights. The number forty often marks a period of testing and preparation in scripture.
On the mountain the Lord begins giving Moses detailed instructions for the tabernacle — a portable temple where He would dwell among His people. Chapters 25–31 record these instructions.
The materials were to come only from willing givers. God wanted offerings given freely from the heart, not taxes forced from the people.
The list of materials begins with metals. Much of this wealth likely came from the Egyptians when Israel left Egypt.

f.g: Really bronze or copper; brass as we know it was not yet in use.

chapters.n: Next come costly dyed yarns, fine linen, and goat hair for the curtains and priestly clothing. Blue, purple, and scarlet dyes were expensive marks of royalty.

f.g: A blue-violet dye made from sea snails.
Woven into tough, dark tent cloth.

chapters.n: Leather coverings and a durable desert wood complete the structural materials.

f.g: Hebrew taḥash; uncertain — possibly fine leather or the hide of a sea animal such as a dugong.
Acacia, a hard, lasting wood that grows in the Sinai desert.

chapters.n: Olive oil fueled the lamps, and spices were blended into sacred anointing oil and incense.
Precious stones were needed for the high priest’s ephod and breastplate, described in chapter 28.

f.g: An apron-like sacred vestment worn by the high priest.

chapters.n: Here is the heart of it all: God wants a holy place so that He can live among His people. The tabernacle, and later temples, exist so heaven and earth can meet.

f.w: that I may dwell among them

chapters.n: Everything must be built exactly according to the heavenly pattern God shows Moses. Hebrews teaches that the earthly tabernacle was a copy of heavenly realities.
The most sacred object comes first: the ark, a chest of acacia wood about 3¾ by 2¼ by 2¼ feet. It would sit in the innermost room, the Holy of Holies.

f.g: A chest or box (a different Hebrew word from Noah’s ark).
A cubit was about 18 inches, the length from elbow to fingertip.

chapters.n: The ark was covered inside and out with pure gold, with a gold molding around the top. Ordinary wood made glorious by gold has been seen by some as an image of humanity joined with divinity.
Four gold rings, two on each side, were attached at the ark’s feet for carrying.
The carrying poles were made of acacia wood covered with gold.
The poles slid through the rings so the ark could be carried — it was never to be touched directly.
The poles were to stay in the rings permanently, ready to travel whenever God’s presence led Israel onward.

f.w: they shall not be taken from it

chapters.n: Inside the ark went “the testimony” — the stone tablets of the law, God’s covenant witness. Later a pot of manna and Aaron’s budding rod were kept with it.

f.g: The tablets bearing the Ten Commandments, which testified to the covenant.

chapters.n: A solid gold lid, the “mercy seat,” covered the ark. Once a year the high priest sprinkled atoning blood on it — a powerful symbol of Christ’s Atonement.

f.g: Hebrew kapporet, related to kipper, “to atone” or “cover”; the place of atonement.

chapters.n: Two golden cherubim were hammered out of the same piece of gold as the lid, one at each end.

f.g: Cherubim are heavenly beings who guard God’s holy presence (the KJV adds an extra English plural -s).
Hammered from one piece of metal.

chapters.n: The cherubim formed one piece with the mercy seat, standing at its two ends.
Their wings stretched upward and over the lid, and their faces looked down toward the mercy seat, as if in reverent attention to the place of atonement.

f.w: stretch forth their wings on high

chapters.n: The mercy seat rested on top of the ark, covering the tablets of the law. Symbolically, mercy covers the law.
This is why the ark mattered: there, between the cherubim above the mercy seat, God would meet and speak with Moses. The place of atonement is the place of communion with God.

f.w: there I will meet with thee

chapters.n: Next, a table about 3 feet long, 1½ feet wide, and 2¼ feet high was to stand in the Holy Place, the first room of the tabernacle.
Like the ark, the table was covered with gold and edged with a gold molding.
A rim about a handbreadth (roughly 3 inches) wide ran around it, also trimmed with gold, perhaps to keep items from sliding off.

f.g: The width of a palm, about 3 inches.

chapters.n: Gold rings were attached at the table’s four legs for carrying.
The rings sat near the rim to hold the carrying poles.
The table’s poles were also gold-covered acacia wood, so it could travel with Israel.
Pure gold dishes, ladles, jars, and bowls were made for the table, likely for incense and drink offerings.

f.g: Small ladles or pans, perhaps for incense.
Better, “to pour with” — vessels for drink offerings.

chapters.n: Bread was always kept on the table in God’s presence — twelve loaves, one for each tribe. Jesus called Himself “the bread of life.”

f.g: “Bread of the Presence” — bread set before the Lord.

chapters.n: A lampstand of pure gold was hammered out of a single piece, with its base, shaft, branches, and decorations all of one piece.

f.g: Hebrew menorah — a lampstand holding oil lamps, not candles.

chapters.n: Three branches curved out from each side of the central shaft, making seven lamps in all.
Each branch was decorated with three cups shaped like almond blossoms. The almond is the first tree to bloom in spring, suggesting life and watchfulness.
The central shaft had four almond-shaped cups with their buds and blossoms.
A bud-shaped knob sat beneath each pair of branches where they joined the shaft.
Everything was to be one hammered piece of pure gold — no joints or seams. The lampstand looked like a golden flowering tree, which some connect with the tree of life.
Seven lamps sat atop the branches, lighting the area in front of it. Since the Holy Place had no windows, this was its only light — a symbol of God’s light and of Christ, the Light of the World.
Even the wick-trimmers and trays for burnt wicks were made of pure gold.
The lampstand and its tools took a full talent of gold — about 75 pounds (34 kg) — showing how precious it was.

f.g: A large unit of weight, roughly 75 pounds.

chapters.n: God repeats the key instruction: build everything exactly according to the pattern shown on the mountain. Temples follow revealed patterns, not human design.
The tabernacle’s innermost covering was ten beautiful linen curtains woven in blue, purple, and scarlet with cherubim designs. Seen from inside, the ceiling would look like the heavenly court.

f.g: Linen made of finely twisted threads.

chapters.n: Each curtain measured about 42 by 6 feet, all the same size.
The ten curtains were sewn into two large sets of five.
Blue loops were sewn along the edge where the two sets would meet.

f.g: The finished edge of woven fabric.

chapters.n: Fifty loops on each edge lined up opposite one another.
Fifty gold clasps joined the two sets so the whole covering became one tabernacle — many parts united as one dwelling.
Over the linen went a tent of goat-hair cloth, the kind of dark, weather-resistant fabric Bedouins still use. It had eleven curtains, one more than the linen layer.
These curtains were slightly longer — about 45 by 6 feet — so they would fully cover the linen beneath.
They were joined into sets of five and six, with the extra sixth curtain folded double at the front entrance.
Like the linen layer, fifty loops lined each joining edge.
Here the clasps were bronze instead of gold — the outer layers used less precious metal, a pattern of increasing holiness toward the center.
The extra half curtain hung down over the back of the tabernacle.
The extra length on each side hung down to cover the sides completely, protecting the linen beneath.
Two more protective layers went on top: red-dyed ram skins and an outer layer of tough leather. From outside the tabernacle looked plain; its beauty was within.

f.g: Hebrew taḥash; meaning uncertain, perhaps durable fine leather or sea-animal hide.

chapters.n: The walls were made of upright frames of acacia wood.

f.g: Possibly open frames rather than solid planks, which would be lighter to carry.

chapters.n: Each frame was about 15 feet tall and 27 inches wide.
Two pegs at the bottom of each frame fit into bases to hold it upright.

f.g: Projecting pegs that fit into sockets.

chapters.n: Twenty frames made up the south wall.
Each frame stood in two silver bases. This silver came from the atonement money paid by each Israelite, so the whole tabernacle literally rested on redemption.

f.g: Heavy bases with holes for the tenons.

chapters.n: Another twenty frames formed the north wall.
These too stood on forty silver bases.
Six frames made up the back (west) wall. The entrance faced east, toward the sunrise.

f.g: Toward the back; the door faced east.

chapters.n: Two special frames reinforced the back corners.
The corner frames were joined at bottom and top with a single ring, making the corners strong.
The back wall thus had eight frames on sixteen silver bases.
Horizontal crossbars of acacia wood held the frames together — five for one side wall.
Five bars likewise braced the other side and the back wall.
The middle bar ran the full length of each wall, tying the whole structure together.
The frames and bars were all covered with gold, with gold rings to hold the bars. Inside, the walls would gleam in the lamplight.
Again the Lord stresses building according to the pattern revealed on the mountain.
A richly woven veil with cherubim was to divide the inner rooms. Cherubim once guarded the way back to Eden; here they guard the way into God’s presence.

f.g: A curtain separating the two inner rooms.

chapters.n: The veil hung by gold hooks from four gold-covered pillars set in silver bases.
The veil hung beneath the clasps, separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, where the ark rested. When Jesus died, the temple veil was torn from top to bottom, opening the way to God.

f.g: Literally “the holy of holies” — the innermost room.

chapters.n: The mercy seat sat atop the ark in the Most Holy Place.
Outside the veil, in the Holy Place, the table of bread stood on the north side and the lampstand on the south.
A colorful embroidered curtain served as the tabernacle’s front door.
This entrance curtain hung on five gold-covered pillars, but their bases were bronze — another reminder that holiness increased as one moved inward.
In the courtyard outside the tent stood the altar of burnt offering, about 7½ feet square and 4½ feet high. It was the first thing a worshipper met: no one approached God without sacrifice.
Horn-shaped projections rose from each corner, and the whole altar was covered with bronze to withstand the fire. Blood was put on the horns, and people seeking mercy sometimes grabbed them.
All the altar’s tools — ash pans, shovels, bowls for blood, meat forks, and fire pans — were made of bronze.

f.g: Large forks for handling sacrificial meat.

chapters.n: A bronze grate of network was made with rings at its four corners.
The grate sat halfway up inside the altar, under its ledge, perhaps holding the fire or forming a supporting rim.
Like the other furniture, the altar had acacia poles, here covered with bronze.
The poles fit through rings on both sides so the altar could be carried as Israel traveled.
The altar was a hollow box made of planks, likely filled with earth or stones when set up, following the pattern Moses was shown.
A courtyard surrounded the tabernacle, fenced with linen curtains. The south side was 100 cubits — about 150 feet — long.
Twenty bronze-based pillars held up the curtains, with silver hooks and bands.

f.g: Bands or connecting rods, possibly joining the tops of the pillars.

chapters.n: The north side matched the south: 100 cubits with twenty pillars.
The back (west) side was 50 cubits — about 75 feet — wide, with ten pillars.
The front (east) side was also 50 cubits wide and held the entrance.

f.g: Toward the sunrise; the entrance faced east.

chapters.n: On one side of the gate was a curtain section 15 cubits wide on three pillars.
A matching 15-cubit section stood on the other side of the gate.
The gate itself was a 20-cubit (30-foot) embroidered curtain in blue, purple, and scarlet — wide and colorful, clearly marking the one way in. Jesus later said, “I am the door.”
All the court pillars had silver bands and hooks and bronze bases.
In total, the courtyard was about 150 feet by 75 feet, enclosed by linen curtains about 7½ feet high — tall enough to mark sacred space.
All the tabernacle’s tools and the tent pegs for the structure and courtyard were bronze.
The people were to supply the purest olive oil, pressed by beating rather than crushing, to keep the lamp burning continually.

f.g: The first, clearest oil, gently crushed from olives in a mortar.

f.w: to cause the lamp to burn always

chapters.n: Aaron and his sons tended the lamp in the Holy Place every night before the Lord. This duty would last for all generations, a symbol of Israel’s constant light before God.

f.g: Better “tent of meeting” — where God met with Israel.

chapters.n: God calls Aaron and his four sons to serve as priests. This is the beginning of the priesthood that Latter-day Saints call the Aaronic or Levitical Priesthood.

f.w: minister unto me in the priest's office

chapters.n: Aaron was to wear sacred clothing “for glory and for beauty” — garments that honored God and dignified the sacred office, not the man.
Skilled artisans whom God had filled with wisdom would make the garments. Craftsmanship itself is presented as a spiritual gift.

f.g: Skilled; in Hebrew the heart is the seat of understanding.

chapters.n: Six garments are listed for the high priest. Each would be described in turn, and simpler versions were made for his sons.

f.g: A tunic of checkered or patterned weave.

chapters.n: The same fine materials used in the tabernacle — gold and colored linen — were used for the garments, so the priest was dressed to match God’s house.
The ephod, an apron-like vestment, was woven with gold thread and colored yarns in skillful designs.

f.g: A sleeveless garment worn over the robe, front and back.

chapters.n: Two shoulder straps joined the front and back of the ephod.
A band woven of the same materials served as the ephod’s waistband.
Two onyx stones were engraved with the names of Jacob’s sons, the tribes of Israel.

f.g: Identification of ancient gems is uncertain; possibly carnelian or another hard stone.

chapters.n: Six names went on each stone in order of birth.
The names were cut like a seal and set in gold settings.

f.g: A seal ring used to stamp a mark of ownership.

chapters.n: The stones sat on Aaron’s shoulders so he “carried” Israel before the Lord. A priest bears the burdens of the people he serves — an image fulfilled in Christ, who carries us.
Gold settings were made to hold the stones.
Braided gold chains attached to these settings would later connect to the breastplate.
The “breastplate of judgment” was a woven pouch worn on the chest, made like the ephod. It was used to seek God’s will for Israel.

f.g: Called so because it held the Urim and Thummim, used to receive God’s decisions.

chapters.n: It was a square of folded fabric about nine inches on each side, doubled to form a pocket.

f.g: The distance from thumb to little finger with the hand spread, about 9 inches.
Folded over to form a pouch.

chapters.n: Twelve precious stones in four rows were set into the breastplate. The exact identity of several gems is uncertain today.

f.g: Probably a red stone such as carnelian.
A glittering stone, perhaps an emerald or garnet.

chapters.n: The second row of three stones.

f.g: Probably not a true diamond, which ancient engravers could not cut; perhaps jasper or onyx.

chapters.n: The third row of three stones.

f.g: An unknown stone, perhaps jacinth or amber.

chapters.n: The fourth row, each stone set in gold. Similar stones adorn the foundations of the New Jerusalem in Revelation.
Each stone was engraved with the name of one tribe. Every tribe — great or small — had its own place.
Braided gold chains were made for the breastplate.
Two gold rings were fixed to the top corners of the breastplate.
The gold chains passed through these upper rings.
The other ends of the chains fastened to the shoulder settings, hanging the breastplate from the shoulders.
Two more gold rings were placed on the lower inside corners of the breastplate.
Matching rings on the front of the ephod, just above its waistband, lined up with them.
A blue cord tied the lower rings together so the breastplate stayed firmly attached to the ephod.
Aaron bore the twelve tribes’ names over his heart whenever he entered the Holy Place. Israel was carried both on his shoulders (strength) and on his heart (love) before God.

The Urim and Thummim were placed in the breastplate — sacred instruments through which God revealed His will. Latter-day Saints know them as instruments like those Joseph Smith received with the gold plates.

f.g: Hebrew, often understood as “lights and perfections.”
f.r: Numbers 27:21; Ezra 2:63; Abraham 3:1; Joseph Smith—History 1:35; D&C 17:1

chapters.n: The robe worn under the ephod was entirely blue, a color associated with heaven.

f.g: A long sleeveless robe worn beneath the ephod.

chapters.n: The robe had a reinforced opening for the head so it would not tear, like the neck of a coat of mail.

f.g: A coat of mail or leather armor.

chapters.n: Around the hem hung pomegranates of colored yarn alternating with golden bells. Pomegranates, full of seeds, suggest fruitfulness and abundance.
The pattern alternated all around the hem: bell, pomegranate, bell, pomegranate.
The bells sounded as Aaron moved in the sanctuary, announcing his presence as he served. He was to approach God only in the prescribed way, with reverence.

f.g: A reminder that God’s presence is holy and must be approached as He directs.

chapters.n: A gold plate engraved “HOLINESS TO THE LORD” was made for the turban. Latter-day Saint temples bear these same words today.
The gold plate was tied with a blue cord to the front of Aaron’s turban.
Wearing it, Aaron bore any guilt connected with Israel’s imperfect offerings so that they could be accepted. In this he foreshadowed Christ, who makes our imperfect offerings acceptable to God.
The tunic and turban were of fine linen, and the sash embroidered.
Aaron’s sons also received tunics, sashes, and caps, likewise “for glory and for beauty.”
Moses was to clothe, anoint, and consecrate them. This sequence — clothing, anointing, setting apart — is carried out in Exodus 29 and Leviticus 8.
Linen undergarments ensured modesty while the priests served.
Priests had to wear these whenever they entered the sanctuary or served at the altar. Reverence and modesty in sacred service were a permanent requirement.

God now explains the ceremony to consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests. It begins with gathering animals for sacrifice — a young bull and two flawless rams. Leviticus 8 records how it was carried out.

f.g: Perfect, with no defect — pointing to Christ’s sinless life.

chapters.n: Three kinds of unleavened bread made from fine wheat flour were also prepared.
The breads were placed in one basket and brought along with the animals.
First, Aaron and his sons were brought to the entrance and washed with water. Washing comes before anointing — a pattern Latter-day Saints recognize in temple ordinances.
Next Moses dressed Aaron in the high priest’s garments, layer by layer.

f.g: Fasten with a belt or sash.

chapters.n: Last came the turban and the holy crown — the gold plate engraved “Holiness to the Lord.”
Moses poured holy anointing oil on Aaron’s head. The title “Messiah” (Hebrew) and “Christ” (Greek) both mean “Anointed One.”
Then Aaron’s sons were brought forward and dressed in their tunics.
With sashes and caps, the sons were clothed, and the priesthood was confirmed to Aaron’s family as a lasting ordinance.
The bull was brought, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head — symbolically transferring their sins to the animal that would die in their place.

f.w: put their hands upon the head

chapters.n: The bull was killed before the Lord at the tabernacle entrance.
Some blood was put on the altar’s horns and the rest poured at its base, cleansing the altar itself.
The fat and certain internal organs — considered the choicest parts — were burned on the altar as belonging to God.

f.g: The fatty lobe or covering of the liver.

chapters.n: The rest of the bull was burned outside the camp because it carried sin. Hebrews notes that Jesus also suffered “without the gate.”

f.g: An offering to cleanse from sin.

chapters.n: Next came the first ram, again with hands laid on its head.
The ram was killed and its blood splashed around the altar.
The ram was cut up and its organs and legs washed before burning.
The entire ram was burned as a burnt offering — total dedication of the priests to God. Its “sweet savour” means God accepted it with pleasure.

f.g: Pleasing aroma — an idiom for an acceptable offering.

chapters.n: The second ram was the “ram of consecration,” and again the priests laid hands on it.
Its blood was dabbed on each priest’s right ear, right thumb, and right big toe — consecrating what they would hear, what they would do, and where they would walk.
Blood and anointing oil were then sprinkled on the priests and their garments, making them holy. Blood (atonement) and oil (the Spirit) together prepared them to serve.
Choice portions of this ram, including the right thigh, were set apart.

f.g: The fat tail, a prized portion in Middle Eastern sheep.
Literally “ram of filling” — from the idiom “fill the hands,” meaning to install someone in office.

chapters.n: One of each kind of bread was taken from the basket.
Moses placed these portions in the priests’ hands and they waved them before the Lord — a gesture of presenting the offering to God. Their hands were literally “filled” for service.

f.g: An offering lifted or moved before the altar to dedicate it to God.

chapters.n: Moses then took the portions and burned them on the altar.
The ram’s breast was waved before the Lord and became Moses’s portion, since he acted as priest in this ceremony.
The breast and thigh were made holy portions belonging to the priests.

f.g: A portion “lifted up” or set aside as a contribution to God, given to the priests.

chapters.n: From then on, the breast and thigh of Israel’s peace offerings would always belong to the priests as their support.
The high priest’s garments would pass to his successor, who would be anointed and consecrated in them.
The new high priest would wear them for seven days of consecration when he began serving.
The meat of the consecration ram was boiled in a holy area.
Aaron and his sons ate the meat and bread at the entrance — a sacred meal sealing their new relationship with God.
Only the priests could eat these atonement offerings; no outsider could share them because they were holy.

f.g: Hebrew kipper — to cover, cleanse, or reconcile.

chapters.n: Any leftovers were burned by morning rather than eaten, keeping the holy food from being treated as ordinary.
The whole ceremony was repeated over seven days, a number that in scripture signals completeness.
Each day a bull was offered to make atonement for the altar itself, cleansing and anointing it.
After seven days the altar became “most holy,” so that whatever touched it became holy too.
God also commanded a daily offering: two year-old lambs every day, without fail.
One lamb was offered in the morning and one in the evening. Israel’s day began and ended with sacrifice, a constant reminder of their need for atonement.
Each lamb was accompanied by flour mixed with olive oil and a drink offering of wine.

f.g: A tenth of an ephah, about two quarts of flour.
A liquid measure of about a gallon (4 liters).
Wine poured out at the altar.

chapters.n: The evening lamb was offered with the same grain and drink offerings as the morning one.

f.g: Grain offering; in KJV English “meat” means food in general.

chapters.n: This continual offering would be made for all generations at the tent of meeting — the place where God promised to meet and speak with His people.
God promises to meet Israel there and to make the tabernacle holy by His own glory. His presence is what makes a place holy.
God Himself would make holy the tent, the altar, and the priests. Ordinances are performed by people, but sanctification comes from God.
Here is the goal of the whole tabernacle: God dwelling among His people as their God.

f.w: I will dwell among the children of Israel

chapters.n: Israel would come to know the Lord as the God who freed them from Egypt for this very purpose — so He could live among them. Redemption leads to relationship.

f.w: that I may dwell among them

chapters.n: A small altar for burning incense was to be made of acacia wood. It stood in the Holy Place, closest of all the furniture to the veil and God’s presence.
It was small — about 18 inches square and 3 feet tall — with horns at its corners like the great altar outside.
Unlike the bronze altar outside, it was covered with pure gold and edged with a gold molding, fitting its place inside the sanctuary.
Two gold rings on its sides held the carrying poles.
Its poles were gold-covered acacia wood.
It stood just in front of the veil, facing the ark and mercy seat on the other side — the place where God met with Moses.
Every morning when Aaron trimmed the lamps, he burned fragrant incense on this altar.
Incense was burned again each evening, so a fragrant cloud rose before the Lord continually. Scripture often compares incense to the prayers of the faithful.
Only the prescribed incense could be burned there — no unauthorized incense and no other kinds of offerings. Leviticus 10 shows the seriousness of this rule.

f.g: Unauthorized incense not made by God’s recipe.

chapters.n: Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, the high priest put sacrificial blood on this altar’s horns to cleanse it.
The Lord gives Moses another instruction.
When Israel was counted, each man had to pay a “ransom for his soul.” Being counted as one of God’s people required acknowledging that one’s life was redeemed by Him.

f.g: A payment to redeem one’s life.

chapters.n: Each person paid half a shekel by the sanctuary standard. Later Jews paid a temple tax based on this, which Jesus also paid.

f.g: The official standard weight used at the sanctuary.
A small unit of weight; twenty made a shekel.

chapters.n: Every man twenty years or older — the age of military service — had to give.
The rich paid no more and the poor no less. Every soul has equal worth before God, and all need the same redemption.

f.w: The rich shall not give more

chapters.n: This atonement money was used for the tabernacle. Exodus 38 says the silver went into the bases of the walls, so the house of God literally stood on the people’s redemption.
The Lord continues His instructions.
A bronze basin on a stand was placed between the altar and the tent, filled with water for washing.
Aaron and his sons washed their hands and feet there before serving.
They had to wash before entering the tent or serving at the altar. Approaching God required being clean.
Washing hands (what we do) and feet (where we walk) was a permanent rule for all priests. Clean hands and a pure heart remain the requirement for standing in holy places.
The Lord now gives the recipe for the sacred anointing oil.
The finest spices were to be used: liquid myrrh, fragrant cinnamon, and aromatic cane, measured by weight.

f.g: A fragrant resin from a desert shrub.

chapters.n: Cassia (a cinnamon-like bark) was added to about a gallon of olive oil.

f.g: An aromatic bark related to cinnamon.

chapters.n: These were blended by an expert perfumer into holy anointing oil.
The oil was used to anoint the tent and the ark.
It also anointed the table, lampstand, incense altar, and their utensils.
Even the outer altar and the laver were anointed.
Anointing made each item “most holy,” set apart wholly for God.

f.w: whatsoever toucheth them shall be holy

chapters.n: Aaron and his sons were anointed with the same oil, consecrating them as priests.
This oil was to remain uniquely holy for all generations.
It could not be used on ordinary people or copied for personal use. Sacred things must not be treated as common.
Anyone who copied it or used it on an unauthorized person would be cut off from Israel.

f.g: Here, anyone who is not a priest.
Excluded from the covenant community, and possibly put to death.

chapters.n: Next is the recipe for the sacred incense: three rare fragrant ingredients and pure frankincense, in equal amounts.

f.g: A fragrant gum resin, perhaps from the storax tree.
Possibly from a mollusk shell that gives off fragrance when burned.

chapters.n: The perfumer blended them, salted them, and made them pure and holy.
Some was ground fine and placed before the ark in the tent where God met Moses.
Like the oil, this incense was not to be made for personal use; it belonged to the Lord.
Anyone who made it just to enjoy the scent would be cut off. Holy things are given for worship, not personal pleasure.
Having given the tabernacle’s design, the Lord now names the people who will build it.
God personally calls Bezaleel of the tribe of Judah by name. His grandfather Hur may be the same Hur who held up Moses’s arms in battle.

f.g: Name means “in the shadow (protection) of God.”

chapters.n: Bezaleel is the first person in the Bible said to be “filled with the spirit of God” — and for artistic skill. Craftsmanship, too, can be a gift of the Spirit.
He was gifted to design artistic works and to work in precious metals.
He could also cut and set stones and carve wood — every craft the tabernacle required.
Aholiab of the tribe of Dan was appointed as his partner, and God gave skill to many other craftsmen. Judah, a leading tribe, and Dan, a lesser one, worked side by side.
They were to make the tent of meeting, the ark and its mercy seat, and all the tabernacle’s furnishings.
The list covers the table, the lampstand of pure gold, and the incense altar with their tools.
It also includes the bronze altar and the laver with its stand.
The craftsmen would also make the woven cloths and the priestly garments.

f.g: Possibly finely woven garments, or the cloths used to cover sacred items when moving camp.

chapters.n: Finally they would prepare the anointing oil and incense — everything exactly as commanded.
The Lord ends His instructions about the tabernacle with a reminder about the Sabbath.
Even the holy work of building the tabernacle must stop on the Sabbath. The Sabbath is a sign that the Lord is the one who makes His people holy.
Violating the Sabbath was treated as a grave offense against the covenant, carrying the death penalty.
God repeats the six-days-of-work, seventh-day-of-rest pattern.

f.g: Literally “sabbath of sabbaths” — a complete rest.

chapters.n: The Sabbath is a “perpetual covenant” for Israel through all generations.
The Sabbath points back to creation: God worked six days and rested on the seventh. Keeping it lets people share His rest and remember Him as Creator.

f.w: in six days the LORD made heaven and earth

chapters.n: After forty days on the mountain, God gives Moses the two stone tablets written by His own finger. The narrative now turns back to the camp, where something has gone terribly wrong.
While Moses is on the mountain for forty days, the people grow impatient and ask Aaron to make them gods to lead them. Within weeks of promising obedience, they turn away.

f.g: Literally “was ashamed” or slow — long overdue.

chapters.n: Aaron asks for their gold earrings — perhaps hoping the cost would discourage them, though it did not.
The people readily give up their gold. Some of the same treasure would later be offered for the tabernacle.
Aaron shapes the gold into a calf, and the people proclaim it the god who brought them out of Egypt. Bull images were common in Egyptian and Canaanite religion.

f.g: A young bull image cast in metal, likely wood overlaid with gold.

chapters.n: Aaron builds an altar and announces “a feast to the LORD,” trying to mix the worship of Jehovah with an idol. Blending true worship with false gods is still idolatry.
The people offer sacrifices, feast, and then “rise up to play” — likely wild revelry that may have included immoral pagan practices. Paul quotes this verse as a warning.

f.g: Revelry; the Hebrew can imply sexual immorality.

chapters.n: The Lord tells Moses to go down, calling Israel “thy people” — as if distancing Himself from them after they had broken the covenant.
They had abandoned God’s way quickly, breaking the first two commandments within days of hearing them.
God calls Israel “stiffnecked” — like an ox that refuses to bend its neck to the yoke and be guided.
God says He could destroy the nation and start over with Moses. The words “let me alone” may actually invite Moses to intercede and show his heart as a mediator.

f.g: Leave me be — though it may test whether Moses would plead for the people.

f.w: make of thee a great nation

chapters.n: Moses pleads for the people, reminding the Lord that they are His people whom He redeemed with great power.
Moses argues that destroying Israel would let the Egyptians mock God’s purposes. The JST changes this verse so it is the people who must repent, not God.

f.g: JST: “Thy people will repent of this evil; therefore come thou not out against them.” Here “evil” means disaster, not sin.

chapters.n: Moses appeals to God’s covenant promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Effective prayer often pleads God’s own promises back to Him.
The Lord holds back the destruction. The JST clarifies that God would spare those who repented, while those who would not repent would face judgment.

f.g: Relented, changed course. JST: “If they will repent of the evil which they have done, I will spare them.”

chapters.n: Moses descends carrying the two tablets, inscribed on both sides.
The tablets themselves and the writing on them were the direct work of God — making what happens next all the more tragic.

f.w: the writing was the writing of God

chapters.n: Joshua, who had waited partway up the mountain, hears shouting and thinks it is battle.
Moses recognizes it is neither victory nor defeat — it is singing, the noise of revelry.
Seeing the calf and dancing, Moses in righteous anger smashes the tablets — a visible sign that Israel had shattered the covenant.
Moses burns the idol, grinds it to powder, scatters it on the water, and makes the people drink it. Their “god” is shown to be powerless — something that can be swallowed and passed away.
Moses confronts Aaron, who as leader bore responsibility for letting the people sin.
Aaron deflects, blaming the people’s bent toward evil.
He repeats the people’s demand as if it excused him.
Aaron’s excuse is almost comic: he threw in the gold “and there came out this calf” — as if it made itself. Verse 4 says he shaped it. Excuses often hide our own part in sin.
The people were out of control, and Aaron had let them become a disgrace before their enemies.

f.g: Better “running wild” or “unrestrained”; the Hebrew suggests letting loose.

chapters.n: Moses calls for a choice: “Who is on the LORD’s side?” The tribe of Levi responds. Their loyalty here helps explain why Levi later received the priestly service.

f.w: Who is on the LORD's side?

chapters.n: The Levites are sent through the camp to execute judgment on the rebels, even close relatives. This severe judgment reflects how deadly covenant-breaking was to the whole nation.
About three thousand men died that day. Strikingly, on the day of Pentecost about three thousand souls were saved.
By putting loyalty to God above family, the Levites were set apart for His service and received a blessing.

f.g: Literally “fill your hands” — an idiom for ordination to service.

f.w: upon his son, and upon his brother

chapters.n: The next day Moses tells the people their sin is great, but he will go to the Lord and seek atonement for them.
Moses honestly confesses Israel’s sin before the Lord.
Moses offers himself: forgive them, or blot me out of your book. His unfinished sentence shows deep emotion. He mirrors Christ, the true Mediator who gave Himself for His people.

f.w: thy book which thou hast written
f.g: The book of life — the record of God’s people.

chapters.n: God replies that each person answers for his own sin; Moses cannot substitute for them. Only Christ could truly bear others’ sins.
Moses is told to lead the people on, with God’s Angel going before them, but the consequences of their sin will still come.

f.w: mine Angel shall go before thee

f.g: Here, to punish or hold accountable.

chapters.n: The Lord sent a plague because of the calf Aaron made. Sin brings consequences even when mercy spares the nation.
After the golden calf, God tells Moses to lead the people on to the promised land. He will keep His promise to the patriarchs — but notice He again calls them the people Moses brought up.

f.w: Unto thy seed will I give it

chapters.n: An angel will go ahead of them and drive out the nations of Canaan.
Then comes the hard news: God Himself will not go among them, lest His holiness destroy such a rebellious people. The gift of the land without God’s presence would be a tragic loss.

f.g: A picture of rich, fertile land.

chapters.n: The people mourn when they hear this, and they take off their jewelry as a sign of grief and repentance.

f.g: Jewelry, finery — perhaps like the gold used for the calf.

chapters.n: God commands them to remove their ornaments while He decides what to do — an invitation to humility and repentance.

f.w: that I may know what to do unto thee

chapters.n: The Israelites stripped off their ornaments at Mount Horeb (another name for Sinai) and apparently did not wear them again during this time.

Before the tabernacle was built, Moses used a tent pitched outside the camp as a meeting place with God. Placing it outside showed that sin had distanced God from the camp, yet anyone who sought the Lord could still go out to Him.

f.g: Here a temporary tent of meeting, not the tabernacle described in chapters 25–31.

chapters.n: Whenever Moses went to the tent, the people stood at their own tent doors and watched him with reverence.
The pillar of cloud descended to the tent’s door, and the Lord spoke with Moses there.
Seeing the cloud, the people worshipped at their own doors. Their reverence was a sign of returning hearts.
The Lord spoke with Moses “face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend” — a remarkable intimacy. Joshua remained at the tent, being prepared for future leadership.
Moses respectfully presses God: You told me to lead this people, but not who will go with us. Yet You said You know me by name and I have found grace in Your sight.

f.g: A phrase of personal, chosen relationship.

chapters.n: Moses asks to know God’s ways so he might know God better, and he reminds the Lord that Israel is still His people. Knowing God is the heart of eternal life.
God promises, “My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest.” Moses’s intercession has restored what the people had lost.
Moses says that without God’s presence, he would rather not go at all. The promised land meant nothing without the Lord.
What makes Israel different from every other nation is not land or power but God’s presence with them.
The Lord grants Moses’s request because of their personal relationship.
Moses makes the boldest request of all: “Shew me thy glory.” He longs to see God more fully.
God promises to show His goodness and proclaim His name. His glory is revealed first in His character — His grace and mercy, freely given. Paul quotes this verse.

f.w: proclaim the name of the LORD
will shew mercy on whom I will shew mercy

chapters.n: No one in Moses’s condition could see God’s full face and live. The JST adds that this was because of the people’s sinfulness at that time, and that no sinful man can see God’s face and live.

f.w: there shall no man see me, and live
f.g: JST adds “at this time” and explains that no sinful man can see God’s face and live.

chapters.n: God provides a place beside Him where Moses can stand on a rock. Scripture often calls God Himself the Rock of salvation.
God will hide Moses in a cleft of the rock and cover him with His hand as His glory passes by — protecting him even while revealing Himself.
Moses will see God’s “back” — a partial glimpse, like seeing where someone has just passed. This shows both God’s nearness and how much of Him remains beyond mortal sight.

f.g: The back; what remains visible after someone passes.

chapters.n: God mercifully renews the broken covenant. This time Moses must cut the stone tablets himself, and God will write on them. The JST and D&C 84 teach that the second tablets carried a lesser law than the first, because Israel had rejected the higher one.

f.g: JST adds that the new tablets would not contain the higher priesthood law, but “the law of a carnal commandment.”

chapters.n: Moses is to be ready early in the morning and meet the Lord at the summit.
This time no one else may come up, not even animals may graze near the mountain — a reminder of the holiness of God’s presence.

f.w: no man shall come up with thee

chapters.n: Moses obeys exactly, rising early and carrying the new tablets up the mountain.
The Lord descends in the cloud and proclaims His name — fulfilling His promise in chapter 33 to reveal His goodness to Moses.

f.w: proclaimed the name of the LORD

chapters.n: God describes Himself: merciful, gracious, patient, and full of steadfast love and faithfulness. This self-description is quoted again and again throughout the Old Testament.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed and emet — covenant love and faithfulness.

chapters.n: He forgives every kind of sin, yet He does not pretend sin is harmless. The effects of sin can ripple through families for generations, especially, as the D&C clarifies, among those who keep rejecting Him.

f.g: Three words covering crookedness, rebellion, and missing the mark.

f.w: unto the third and to the fourth generation

chapters.n: Overwhelmed by this revelation of God’s character, Moses quickly bows to the ground in worship.
Moses pleads for God to go with His people, pardon them, and take them as His own inheritance. He includes himself: “our iniquity.”
God renews the covenant and promises unprecedented wonders that will show all nations His work.
Israel must obey, and God will drive out the nations of Canaan.
They must not make treaties with the Canaanites, who would become a trap.
All Canaanite religious objects must be destroyed.

f.g: Hebrew asherim — wooden poles honoring the goddess Asherah.

chapters.n: God is “jealous” — not petty, but passionately committed to His people, like a faithful spouse who will not share them with rivals.

f.g: The JST reads “Jehovah” here: “the Lord, whose name is Jehovah.”

chapters.n: Making alliances with Canaanites would lead to sharing their sacrifices. Idolatry is described as spiritual adultery — unfaithfulness to the covenant God.

f.g: A metaphor for unfaithfulness to God through idolatry.

chapters.n: Intermarriage with idol-worshippers would draw Israel’s sons away from God, as later happened even to Solomon.

f.w: take of their daughters unto thy sons

chapters.n: A direct echo of the golden calf: no cast-metal gods.
God repeats key covenant laws, beginning with the Feast of Unleavened Bread remembering the Exodus.

f.g: The spring month of the Exodus.

chapters.n: Every firstborn male belongs to the Lord.

f.g: First to open the womb — the firstborn.

chapters.n: Unclean animals like donkeys and all firstborn sons were redeemed with a payment or substitute. Worshippers were not to come before God empty-handed.

f.g: Buy back by a substitute or payment.

chapters.n: The Sabbath must be kept even during the busiest farming seasons, when stopping would seem most costly.
Two harvest festivals are commanded: the Feast of Weeks in early summer and the Feast of Ingathering in the fall.
All males must appear before the Lord three times a year.
God promises that while the men are away at the feasts, no one will seize their land. Obedience is rewarded with protection.

f.w: neither shall any man desire thy land
f.g: God would guard their homes while they worshipped.

chapters.n: Leaven was not offered with sacrificial blood, and the Passover sacrifice was not left until morning.

f.g: Yeast, often a symbol of corruption.

chapters.n: The firstfruits belong to God, and a young goat is not to be boiled in its mother’s milk.
Moses is told to write down these words, which form the terms of the renewed covenant.
Moses spends another forty days with the Lord without food or water — sustained by God’s presence. The ten commandments were written on the tablets.

f.g: Verse 1 says God would write; Deuteronomy 10:4 confirms the Lord wrote them.

chapters.n: Coming down, Moses did not realize his face was shining from being in God’s presence.

f.g: Hebrew qaran, related to “horn” — rays of light. The Latin Vulgate’s “horned” led to Michelangelo’s horned Moses.

chapters.n: Seeing his radiant face, Aaron and the people were afraid to approach him.
Moses called them back, and the leaders returned and listened.
Then all Israel came near, and Moses taught them everything the Lord had commanded.
After speaking with them, Moses covered his face with a veil.
He removed the veil when he went in before the Lord and when delivering God’s words, then covered his face again afterward.
Paul later used this veil as a symbol: the glory of the old covenant faded, while those who turn to Christ behold God’s glory with unveiled faces and are transformed.

f.w: put the veil upon his face again

chapters.n: With the covenant renewed, Moses gathers all Israel to pass on what the Lord commanded. Chapters 35–40 tell how the people actually built what was described in chapters 25–31 — the repetition stresses their exact obedience.
Moses begins with the Sabbath: even the sacred construction work must pause on the seventh day.
No fires were to be lit in their homes on the Sabbath — likely meaning fires for work such as cooking or metalwork.
Moses now relays the Lord’s command about the offering.
Anyone with a willing heart could bring gold, silver, or bronze. The offering was entirely voluntary.
Dyed yarns, linen, and goat hair were needed for the curtains and garments.
Leather and acacia wood would provide coverings and structure.
Oil and spices were needed for the lamp, the anointing oil, and incense.
Precious stones were requested for the high priest’s ephod and breastplate.
All skilled people were invited to come and help make everything the Lord commanded. Both giving and serving were needed.
Moses lists the tabernacle’s structure: the tent, its coverings, clasps, frames, bars, pillars, and bases.
Then the ark with its poles and mercy seat, and the veil that screened it.

f.g: The screening curtain before the Most Holy Place.

chapters.n: The table, its utensils, and the bread of the Presence.
The lampstand with its tools, lamps, and oil.
The incense altar, anointing oil, incense, and the entrance curtain.
The bronze altar with its grate, poles, and tools, plus the laver and stand.
The courtyard curtains, pillars, bases, and gate screen.
Even the tent pegs and cords are listed — every humble part of God’s house mattered.
Finally, the woven cloths and the sacred garments for Aaron and his sons.

f.g: Finely woven garments or covering cloths.

chapters.n: The people leave Moses to go and gather their offerings.
Everyone whose heart moved them came with offerings for the tent, its service, and the holy garments. Their giving flowed from a changed heart after the golden calf.
Men and women alike gave their gold jewelry. Gold once misused for an idol was now offered for true worship.
Those who had dyed yarns, linen, goat hair, or leather brought them.
Others gave silver, bronze, or acacia wood. Each gave what they had.
Skilled women spun yarn and linen by hand and brought it. Their craftsmanship was itself an offering.
Women gifted in this work spun the goat hair, a tough job requiring skill.
The tribal leaders contributed the precious stones for the ephod and breastplate.
They also gave spices and oil for the lamps, anointing oil, and incense.
The summary: every willing man and woman gave freely for the work. The tabernacle was built by consecrated hearts.
Moses announces that the Lord has called Bezaleel of Judah by name to lead the work.
Bezaleel was filled with God’s Spirit — wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and skill.

f.w: filled him with the spirit of God

chapters.n: His gifts included artistic design and metalwork.
He could also cut gems and carve wood for any skilled work.
God also gave Bezaleel and Aholiab the ability to teach others — gifts multiply when they are shared.
They were gifted in every kind of craft — engraving, design, embroidery, and weaving. The work of God draws on many different talents.

f.g: One who decorates fabric with colored thread.

chapters.n: The work begins. Bezaleel, Aholiab, and every skilled worker labor according to all that the Lord commanded — God-given ability joined with obedience.

f.w: according to all that the LORD had commanded

chapters.n: Moses calls the craftsmen — everyone whose heart moved them to take part in the work.
The craftsmen receive the offerings, yet the people keep bringing more freewill gifts every morning.
The craftsmen stop their work to come and speak with Moses.
They report something remarkable: the people are bringing far more than is needed.
Moses has to issue a proclamation asking people to stop giving! The same people who once gave gold for a calf now had to be restrained from giving to God.
There was more than enough material for all the work.
The workers make the ten inner linen curtains with woven cherubim, as commanded in Exodus 26:1.
Each curtain is the same size — about 42 by 6 feet.
The curtains are joined into two sets of five.
Blue loops are sewn along the joining edges.
Fifty loops line up on each edge.
Fifty gold clasps join the sets so that “it became one tabernacle.”
The eleven goat-hair curtains form the tent over the linen.
Each goat-hair curtain measures about 45 by 6 feet.
They are joined into sets of five and six.
Fifty loops are made along each joining edge.
Bronze clasps join the goat-hair tent into one.
The two outer coverings of red ram skins and durable leather are made.
Upright acacia-wood frames are made for the walls.
Each frame is about 15 feet tall and 27 inches wide.
Each frame has two pegs to anchor it into its bases.
Twenty frames form the south wall.
Forty silver bases, two per frame, support them.
Twenty frames form the north wall.
These also stand on forty silver bases.
Six frames make up the western (back) wall.
Two corner frames are made for the back corners.
They are joined at the bottom and top by a single ring for strength.
The back wall totals eight frames on sixteen silver bases.
Five acacia crossbars brace one side wall.
Five more brace the other side, and five the back.
The middle bar runs the full length of the walls, binding the frames together.
The frames and bars are covered with gold, with gold rings for the bars.
The veil, woven in blue, purple, scarlet, and linen with cherubim, is made to divide the Holy Place from the Most Holy.
Four gold-covered acacia pillars on silver bases hold the veil.
An embroidered curtain is made for the tent’s entrance.
Its five pillars have gold-covered tops and bands, but bronze bases — marking the transition from the outer court to the holy tent.
Bezaleel personally crafts the ark, the most sacred object, matching exactly the dimensions God gave in Exodus 25:10.
He covers it inside and out with pure gold and adds a gold rim.
Four gold rings are cast and attached at the corners.
He makes the carrying poles of acacia covered in gold.
The poles go into the rings so the ark can be carried without being touched.
He makes the mercy seat — the place of atonement — of solid pure gold, the same size as the top of the ark.
Two golden cherubim are hammered from the same piece of gold as the mercy seat.

f.g: Hammered from a single piece of metal.

chapters.n: One cherub stands at each end, forming one piece with the lid.
Their wings spread over the mercy seat and their faces turn toward it — a picture of heaven’s attention fixed on the place where atonement is made.
He builds the table for the bread of the Presence from acacia wood.
The table is covered with gold and edged with a gold molding.
A handbreadth-wide frame runs around it, also edged in gold.
Four gold rings are fixed at its legs.
The rings sit near the frame to hold the carrying poles.
The table’s poles are gold-covered acacia.
Pure gold plates, dishes, bowls, and pitchers are made for the table, likely for incense and drink offerings.
The lampstand is hammered from a single piece of pure gold, as commanded in Exodus 25:31.
Six branches extend from its sides, three on each side.
Each branch has three almond-blossom cups with buds and flowers.
The central shaft has four such cups.
A bud sits beneath each pair of branches.
Everything is one hammered piece of pure gold, without joints — a single, unified light.
Its seven lamps and wick-trimming tools are also pure gold.
The lampstand and its tools take a talent of gold — about 75 pounds.
Bezaleel builds the small incense altar of acacia wood with horns on its corners.
He covers its top, sides, and horns with gold and adds a gold rim.
Two gold rings under the rim hold its poles.
Its poles are acacia covered in gold.
Finally he prepares the holy anointing oil and pure incense by the perfumer’s art, following the recipes of Exodus 30.
Attention moves out to the courtyard. Bezaleel builds the great altar of burnt offering, about 7½ feet square and 4½ feet high.
Horns rise from its corners, and the whole is covered in bronze to bear the fire.
All its tools — pots, shovels, bowls, forks, and fire pans — are made of bronze.
A bronze grate is set beneath the altar’s ledge, halfway up.
Four rings are cast for the grate’s corners to hold the poles.
Its poles are acacia covered with bronze.
The poles go through the rings for carrying. The altar is a hollow box of planks.
The bronze laver is made from the polished bronze mirrors given by women who served at the tent’s entrance. Their personal treasures became a basin for cleansing.

f.g: Women who served at the entrance of the tent.

chapters.n: The courtyard is enclosed with linen curtains — the south side 100 cubits (about 150 feet) long.
Twenty pillars on bronze bases, with silver hooks and bands, hold up the south side.
The north side matches it: 100 cubits on twenty pillars.
The back (west) side is 50 cubits with ten pillars.
The front (east) side is also 50 cubits.
On one side of the gate hang 15 cubits of curtain on three pillars.
The other side of the gate matches with 15 cubits on three pillars.

f.w: on this hand and that hand

chapters.n: All the courtyard curtains are of fine twisted linen — white, clean, and bright.
The pillars have bronze bases with silver hooks, bands, and caps.
The gate is a 30-foot embroidered curtain in blue, purple, and scarlet, matching the height of the courtyard walls.
Four pillars on bronze bases with silver fittings support the gate.
All tent pegs for the tabernacle and courtyard are bronze.
Now comes an inventory of materials, recorded for the Levites under the supervision of Aaron’s son Ithamar. Careful accounting of sacred offerings honored the givers’ trust.
Bezaleel made everything the Lord commanded Moses — a phrase that underlines faithful obedience.
Aholiab of Dan assisted as engraver, designer, and embroiderer.
The gold offered totaled 29 talents and 730 shekels — roughly a ton of gold.

f.g: A talent was about 75 pounds; it held 3,000 shekels.

chapters.n: The silver came from the census tax and totaled 100 talents and 1,775 shekels — several tons.
Each man twenty and older paid half a shekel. The total of 603,550 men matches the census in Numbers 1.

f.w: six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty men

chapters.n: The silver was cast into the 100 bases for the tabernacle walls and veil pillars — one talent per base. God’s house rested on the ransom paid for His people.
The remaining silver made the hooks, caps, and bands for the court pillars.
The bronze offered totaled 70 talents and 2,400 shekels.
It was used for the entrance bases, the bronze altar and its grate, and all its tools.
It also made the courtyard bases, gate bases, and all the tent pegs — every part accounted for.
The craftsmen make the woven cloths and Aaron’s sacred garments. The phrase “as the LORD commanded Moses” appears seven times in the garment section of this chapter, emphasizing complete obedience.
The ephod is woven with gold thread and colored linen.
Gold was hammered into thin sheets and cut into threads to weave into the fabric — a detail showing the painstaking craftsmanship involved.
Shoulder straps join the ephod’s front and back.
Its woven waistband is made of the same materials.
The onyx stones are set in gold and engraved like seals with the names of Israel’s sons.
They are placed on the ephod’s shoulders as a memorial — Aaron carries Israel before the Lord.
The breastplate is woven like the ephod.
It is square and folded double, a span on each side.
Four rows of precious stones are set in it, the first being sardius, topaz, and carbuncle.
The second row: emerald, sapphire, and diamond (the ancient names are uncertain).
The third row: ligure, agate, and amethyst.
The fourth row: beryl, onyx, and jasper, each set in gold.
Each of the twelve stones bears the name of a tribe.
Braided chains of pure gold are made for the breastplate.
Two gold settings and two gold rings are made, with the rings on the breastplate’s top corners.
The chains are threaded through the upper rings.
The chains’ other ends attach to the shoulder settings at the front.
Two more rings are placed on the lower inside corners of the breastplate.
Matching rings are fixed on the front of the ephod above the waistband.
A blue cord ties the rings together so the breastplate stays secure.
The robe worn beneath the ephod is woven entirely of blue.
Its neck opening is reinforced so it will not tear.
Colorful pomegranates of yarn decorate the hem.
Golden bells are placed between the pomegranates.
The alternating bell and pomegranate run all around the hem, worn when Aaron ministered.
Woven linen tunics are made for Aaron and his sons.
Linen turbans, caps, and undergarments complete their clothing.
The embroidered sash is made of linen and colored yarn.
The gold plate for the turban is engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD — words now inscribed on Latter-day Saint temples.
It is fastened high on the turban with a blue cord.
The work is finished. Israel did everything the Lord commanded — the people who broke the covenant with the calf now carefully keep it.
The people bring all the finished pieces to Moses, beginning with the tent and its framework.
The coverings and the veil are presented.
Then the ark with its poles and mercy seat.
The table, its utensils, and the bread of the Presence.
The pure gold lampstand with its lamps arranged, its tools, and oil.
The golden incense altar, the oil, the incense, and the entrance curtain.
The bronze altar with its grate, poles, and tools, plus the laver and its base.
The courtyard curtains, pillars, bases, gate screen, cords, and pegs — everything needed for the service.
Finally the woven cloths and the sacred garments for the priests.
Israel made everything exactly according to the Lord’s command.
Moses inspects the work, finds it done just as the Lord commanded, and blesses the people. The scene echoes creation, when God saw all He had made and called it very good.

f.w: Moses did look upon all the work

chapters.n: With all the pieces finished, the Lord gives Moses instructions for setting up the tabernacle.
It was to be raised on New Year’s Day — the first day of the first month, almost exactly a year after Israel left Egypt. A new beginning for a redeemed people.

f.w: first day of the first month

chapters.n: The ark goes in first, screened off by the veil. The order moves from the most holy center outward.

f.w: cover the ark with the veil
f.g: Screen it off behind the veil.

chapters.n: The table is brought in with its bread arranged, and the lampstand is lit.
The gold incense altar is placed before the ark, outside the veil, and the entrance curtain is hung.
The bronze altar of burnt offering stands in front of the entrance — the first thing a worshipper would encounter.
The laver goes between the tent and the altar and is filled with water.
The courtyard walls are set up and the gate curtain hung.
Moses is to anoint the tabernacle and everything in it to make it holy.
The altar of burnt offering and its tools are anointed, making it most holy.
The laver and its stand are anointed too.
Aaron and his sons are brought to the entrance and washed with water.
Aaron is clothed in the holy garments, anointed, and set apart to serve as priest.
His sons are brought and clothed in their tunics.
They too are anointed, and their anointing establishes a lasting priesthood through their generations. Latter-day Saints teach that this Aaronic Priesthood was restored in 1829.
Moses does everything just as the Lord commanded. (The consecration of the priests is carried out in Leviticus 8.)
On the first day of the second year after the Exodus, the tabernacle is raised.
Moses sets the bases, frames, bars, and pillars in place.
He spreads the tent coverings over the structure.
He places the testimony (the tablets of the covenant) inside the ark, inserts the poles, and sets the mercy seat on top.
He carries the ark into the tabernacle and hangs the veil to screen it.
The table is placed on the north side of the Holy Place, outside the veil.
Moses arranges the bread before the Lord.
The lampstand is placed on the south side, opposite the table.
He lights the lamps before the Lord.
The golden incense altar is set before the veil.
He burns fragrant incense on it.
The entrance curtain is hung.
The bronze altar is set at the entrance, and Moses offers the first burnt and grain offerings on it.
The laver is placed and filled with water for washing.
Moses, Aaron, and his sons wash their hands and feet there.
They wash whenever they enter the tent or approach the altar, as commanded.
Moses sets up the courtyard and gate. “So Moses finished the work” echoes the language of God finishing creation.
The climax of Exodus: the cloud covers the tent and the glory of the Lord fills the tabernacle. God now dwells among His people, just as He promised.

f.w: the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle

chapters.n: God’s glory was so overwhelming that even Moses could not enter. The holiness that once rested on Sinai now rested in the camp.

f.w: Moses was not able to enter

chapters.n: From then on, when the cloud lifted from the tabernacle, Israel moved on.
If the cloud stayed, they stayed — however long that took. Israel learned to move on God’s timing, not their own.

Day and night, cloud and fire over the tabernacle assured all Israel that God was with them throughout their journeys. The book that began in slavery ends with God dwelling in the midst of His people.
